author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Ellipsis and substitution: leaving words out and replacing them
summary: Fluent speakers avoid repeating words. They replace them with so, not, one, do or that, or simply leave them out. These tools make speech and writing concise and cohesive.

blocks.text: Good English avoids repeating what the listener already knows. **Substitution** replaces a word or phrase with a short form (*one, so, do, not*); **ellipsis** leaves it out entirely. Both make speech and writing more natural and more cohesive.

Replace or leave out only what the listener can recover **unambiguously**. Nouns → *one/ones*. Clauses → *so/not* (*I think so, I hope not*). Verb phrases → an auxiliary (*She said she'd help, and she **did***).

items.en: "Is it going to rain?" "I hope **not**."
I wanted a large coffee, but they only had small **ones**.
"Coming tonight?" "Can't, sorry."
items.note: informal ellipsis: *Are you* and *I* are left out

blocks.text: **Substitution** replaces a word or phrase with a shorter form; **ellipsis** leaves it out completely because the listener can recover it from context.

items.en: "Is it going to rain?" "I hope **not**."
I wanted a large coffee but they only had small **ones**.
She said she'd help, and she **did**.
"Coming tonight?" "Can't, sorry."
items.note: Ellipsis in informal speech: *Are you* and *I* are left out.

blocks.text: Only leave out or replace what the listener can recover **unambiguously** from the text or situation.

head: Replaces
Substitute
Example
rows: This chair is broken — take the other **one**.
a clause after think, hope, expect, suppose, be afraid, guess
He promised to call, and he **did**. / If you want to leave, **do so** now.
a verb phrase after modals and auxiliaries
I didn't want to go, but I had **to**.

blocks.text: Negative forms with so/not

items: After **and, but, or** you can leave out a repeated subject or auxiliary: *She opened the letter **and** (she) read it twice.*
In comparisons: *He earns more than I do / than me.*
After **wh-** words: *Someone's taken my pen, but I don't know **who**.*
In replies: *"Where are you going?" "(I'm going to the) Library."*

blocks.text: In informal speech, the start of a sentence is often dropped (*situational ellipsis*): *(Have you) Seen Tom? / (It) Sounds good. / (I'll) See you later.* Don't use this in essays.

blocks.title: Ellipsis with auxiliaries: which one to keep?

blocks.text: Keep the **first** auxiliary from the original verb phrase:

items.en: "Have you been waiting long?" "Yes, I **have**."
He said it would be finished, and it **will (be)**.
"Should it have been sent?" "It **should have (been)**."

sections.title: so vs it, one vs it, do so vs do it

head: Compare
Meaning
Example
rows: I lost my umbrella, so I bought a new **one**.
I lost my umbrella, but then I found **it**.
Visitors wishing to leave early may **do so**.
informal, refers to a specific act
Don't touch the oven — I told you not to **do that**!

blocks.text: *Know*, *sure* and *certain* do not take *so*: ~~I know so~~ → *I know.* ~~I'm sure so~~ → *I'm sure (of it).*

rows.wrong: "Is she coming?" "I don't hope so."
rows.right: "Is she coming?" "I hope not."
rows.why: *Hope* forms its negative with *not*, not with *don't … so*.

rows.wrong: I'd like a one with a balcony.
rows.right: I'd like one with a balcony. / I'd like a big one with a balcony.
rows.why: *A one* is only possible with an adjective: *a big one*.

rows.wrong: "Can you help?" "Yes, I can help it."
rows.right: "Can you help?" "Yes, I can."
rows.why: Answer with the auxiliary alone.

rows.wrong: I didn't want to go, but I had.
rows.right: I didn't want to go, but I had to.
rows.why: Keep *to* when the infinitive is left out.

rows.wrong: "Do you think it will work?" "I think it."
rows.right: "Do you think it will work?" "I think so."
rows.why: *So* replaces a whole clause after *think, hope, expect, suppose*.

blocks.text: In academic writing, substitution prevents repetition and links sentences:

items.en: Many studies have examined online learning. **Those** that included adult learners reported higher drop-out rates.
The government promised to reduce emissions but has not **done so**.
Urban areas grew faster than rural **ones**.
Some participants improved; **others** did not.

blocks.text: *Do so*, *those* and *the former / the latter* are typical of formal writing. *Do it*, *that one* and situational ellipsis are typical of speech.
Replace nouns with **one(s)**, clauses with **so/not**, verb phrases with **do / an auxiliary / to**. Leave words out only when they are easy to recover.

items: *I hope not / I'm afraid not* — never *don't hope so*.
*I know / I'm sure* — never *know so*.
Formal: *do so, those, the former/latter*. Informal: dropped subjects (*Sounds great*).

sentences.text: "Have you finished the budget report?"
"Not yet, but I [[will]] by Friday."
"Do you need the latest figures?" "I think [[so]]."
"The old template is slow. Can I use a newer [[one]]?"
"Is the client unhappy?" "I hope [[not]]."
"Can you send it tonight?" "I'll [[try to]]."
"Thanks, that would be great."

check.prompt: "Will the shop be open on Sunday?" "I'm afraid ___."
check.explanation: *Not* replaces the negative clause after *I'm afraid, I hope, I suppose*.

check.prompt: These shoes are too small. Have you got any bigger ___?
check.explanation: *Ones* replaces a plural countable noun.

check.prompt: She promised to call, but she ___.
check.explanation: The auxiliary alone replaces the verb phrase.

check.prompt: Why is *I'd like to* acceptable as a complete answer to "Would you like to join us?"
check.model: The rest of the verb phrase (*join you*) is clear from the question, so it can be left out; *to* stays to show that an infinitive is understood.
check.explanation: In ellipsis after *to*, the *to* is kept.

produce.prompt: Write a short dialogue (6–8 lines) between two colleagues planning a meeting. Avoid repeating words the other person has just said.
checklist: I used *so* or *not* after *think, hope* or *be afraid*.
I used *one / ones* to replace a noun.
I used an auxiliary alone (*I will, she didn't, we can*) to avoid repetition.
Every replaced or missing word is clear from the context.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Future forms, probability and time clauses
summary: English has no single future tense. The form you choose shows how certain you are, whether something is planned or arranged, and how you see the action at a future moment.

blocks.text: English has no single future tense. Instead, you choose a form that shows **how you see** the future event: as a prediction, a decision, a plan, a fixed arrangement or a timetable. The choice depends on your attitude and your evidence, not on how far away the event is.
*will* = prediction or decision made now · *going to* = plan, or prediction from present evidence · present continuous = arrangement · present simple = timetable.

items.en: Look at those clouds: it**'s going to rain**.
I think it**'ll rain** later.
I**'m meeting** the director at ten.
The train **leaves** at 8.15.

blocks.text: Future meaning is expressed with modal verbs (*will, might*), present forms (*I'm meeting*, *the train leaves*) and semi-modals (*be going to, be about to, be due to*). Each adds a different shade of certainty or planning.

head: Form
Use
Example
rows: *Look at the sky, it**'s going to** rain.*
an action in progress at a future time; polite enquiries
*This time tomorrow I**'ll be flying** to Seoul.*

blocks.text: Use adverbs and phrases to show how likely something is:

head: Certainty
Expression
rows: *will definitely / is bound to / is sure to*
*will probably / is likely to / I expect*
*may / might / could / there's a chance that*
*probably won't / is unlikely to / I doubt whether*

blocks.text: Word order: *probably* comes after *will* but before *won't*: *She'll probably come* / *She probably won't come.*
After **when, as soon as, before, after, until, once, by the time** referring to the future, use a **present** tense, not *will*:

items.en: I'll call you **when** I **get** home.
~~I'll call you when I will get home.~~
Don't leave **until** you**'ve signed** the form.

blocks.text: The same rule applies to **if, unless, provided (that), as long as**.
Time expressions do not choose the future form for you — your **reason** (plan, arrangement, prediction, decision) does. But some expressions strongly prefer particular forms.

head: Expression
Typical form
Example
rows: **By Friday** I'**ll have finished** the draft.
**This time next week** we'**ll be lying** on a beach.
**One day** robots **will do** most of this.
**when, as soon as, until, before, after**
present tense in the time clause

items: *in two weeks* = at the end of that period: *I'll be back in two weeks.*
*within two weeks* = at some point before the end.
*by Friday* = no later than Friday (deadline).
*until Friday* = continuously up to Friday: *I'll be here until Friday.*

items.en: I**'ll** see Tom tomorrow.
I**'m going to** see Tom tomorrow.
I**'m seeing** Tom tomorrow.
**Will you be using** the car tonight?
**Will you use** the car tonight?
items.note: can sound like a request or demand

sections.title: Advanced usage: be + to, future in the past

items: **be about to** (very near future), **be on the point of / on the verge of** + -ing.
**be due to** for scheduled events: *The report is due to be published on Monday.*
**be to** for formal arrangements and instructions: *The president **is to** visit Paris next week. You **are to** report to reception.*
**Future in the past**: *I knew she **would** win. We **were going to** move, but…*
**will** for assumptions about the present: *That**'ll** be the postman.* (See *Uses of will and would*.)

rows.wrong: I will meet my dentist at four tomorrow.
rows.right: I'm seeing my dentist at four tomorrow.
rows.why: A fixed arrangement with another person is normally expressed with the present continuous.

rows.wrong: When I will finish university, I'll travel.
rows.right: When I finish university, I'll travel.
rows.why: After time conjunctions (*when, as soon as, until, before, after*) use a present form, not *will*.

rows.wrong: She will probably not come.
rows.right: She probably won't come.
rows.why: In natural English *probably* goes before *won't* (but after *will*: *She'll probably come*).

rows.wrong: Wait, I'm going to help you with that bag!
rows.right: Wait, I'll help you with that bag!
rows.why: A decision or offer made at the moment of speaking takes *will*, not *going to*.

rows.wrong: Do you come to the party on Saturday?
rows.right: Are you coming to the party on Saturday?
rows.why: Asking about someone's arrangement needs the present continuous; the present simple is for timetables and routines.

blocks.text: Academic writing prefers impersonal forms of prediction: *It is likely that…*, *X is expected to…*, *X is projected to rise by 3%*. Formal notices use *be to* and *be due to*: *The building is due to reopen in spring.*

items: will = prediction/decision now; going to = intention/evidence; present continuous = arrangement; present simple = timetable.
Future continuous = in progress at a future time; future perfect = completed before it.
No *will* after time and condition conjunctions.

sentences.text: The keynote speaker [[arrives]] on Thursday at 6.40 p.m., according to the airline.
I[['m meeting]] her at the airport, and we[['re having]] dinner at the hotel.
Last year the event took place in Vilnius.
Registrations are rising fast, so we[['re going to need]] a bigger room.
sentences.note: *going to*: a prediction based on present evidence

sentences.text: The venue staff were very helpful when we visited.
Don't worry about the badges: I[['ll print]] them tonight.
sentences.note: *will*: a decision and an offer made now

sentences.text: Everyone enjoyed the closing reception.

check.prompt: "The phone's ringing." "Don't move, I ___ it."
check.explanation: A decision made at the moment of speaking takes *will*.

check.prompt: I can't come on Friday: I ___ my cousin at the station.
check.explanation: A fixed arrangement with another person: present continuous.

check.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: I'll call you as soon as I will land.
I'll call you as soon as I land.
I call you as soon as I will land.
check.explanation: After *as soon as* (and other time conjunctions) the verb is in the present.

check.prompt: What is the difference between *It'll rain tomorrow* and *It's going to rain*?
check.model: *It'll rain tomorrow* is a general prediction or opinion. *It's going to rain* is a prediction based on present evidence, such as dark clouds.
check.explanation: *Going to* connects the future to something you can see or know now.

produce.prompt: Write a short message (5–6 sentences) to a friend about next weekend. Include an arrangement, a plan, a prediction, a timetable, and one offer or decision you make while writing.
checklist: I used the present continuous for an arrangement with someone.
I used *going to* for a plan, or for a prediction based on evidence.
I used *will* for a decision or offer made now.
I used the present simple for a timetable and after *when* or *as soon as*.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: The future in the past: was going to, was to, was about to, would
summary: To talk about a past moment's future — plans, predictions, destinies and plans that failed — English shifts future forms into the past. The choice signals whether the future happened.

blocks.text: Sometimes you stand at a point in the past and look **forward** from it. The future-in-the-past forms describe what was planned, expected or destined *at that time*, whether or not it actually happened.
Take an ordinary future form and move it into the past: *will → would*, *am going to → was going to*, *am about to → was about to*, *am to → was to*.

items.en: In 1995 few people imagined that the internet **would** change everything.
I **was going to** call you, but my phone died.
items.note: a plan that was not carried out

blocks.text: The key question is always: *where is the viewpoint?* If it is in the past and you are looking ahead from it, you need one of these forms.

When we narrate or report, we often need to look forward from a point in the past: *In 1990 nobody knew that the internet **would** change everything.* *I **was going to** call you, but my phone died.* *She **was to** become the first woman to lead the institute.* These forms are the past-shifted versions of ordinary future forms. They allow a narrator to show plans, expectations, destinies and **unfulfilled intentions** with precision.

sections.title: How it works: a past viewpoint looking forward

blocks.text: Choose a reference point in the past, then take the future form you would have used at that point and **move it one step back**:

head: At the time (present viewpoint)
Narrated (past viewpoint)
rows: *He promised he **would** see me the next day.*
*The report is due to appear in May.*
*The report **was due to** appear in May.*

blocks.text: Whether the future event actually happened is often left open, or clarified by context or by the **perfect infinitive**: *We **were to have** met at noon* = the meeting was planned but did **not** happen.

*was/were going to* and *was/were to have + past participle* frequently imply that a plan was **not carried out**. *Would* and *was to* + base form, in narrative, often imply that the future **did** happen.

head: Form
Meaning
Example
rows: future seen from the past (prediction, promise)
past intention or prediction; often unfulfilled
*I **was going to** email you, but I forgot.*
was/were about to / on the point of + -ing
*I **was about to** leave when the phone rang. We **were on the point of giving** up.*
*It **was to** be his last film. We **were to** meet at six.*
*The minister **was to have** opened the bridge.*
*I couldn't come — I **was flying** to Rome the next day.*
completed before a future point in the past
*By the end of the year, he hoped, he **would have finished**.*

blocks.text: 1. Reporting predictions and promises
*Everyone thought the reforms **would** fail.* *She promised that she **would** be careful.*
2. Unfulfilled plans and excuses
*I **was going to** finish it last night, but ...* is the standard way to explain a plan that changed. Adding *but* clarifies.
3. Narrative foreshadowing (destiny)

*Was to* and *would* let a narrator reveal the future from a past viewpoint: *Little did he know that this meeting **would** change his life.* *The village **was to** remain isolated for another century.*
4. Interruptions of imminent action
*was about to / was on the point of / was just going to* + *when*: *We **were about to** sign the contract **when** the investor withdrew.*

items.en: At the time, few economists predicted that the crisis **would** spread so quickly.
I **was going to** apply for the scholarship, but the deadline had passed.
The building **was to have** opened in 2020, but construction stalled.
items.note: planned event that did not happen

items.en: Darwin **was to** spend five years on the voyage, a journey that **would** reshape biology.
She **was on the point of** resigning when she was offered a promotion.
The results **were due to** be published in March.
He hoped that by spring he **would have saved** enough for the trip.

head: Pair
Difference
rows: intention/plan (*I was going to tell you*) vs prediction or willingness seen from the past (*I knew you would understand*).
*was to do* vs *was to have done*
arrangement (outcome open, or destiny: it happened) vs arrangement that did not happen.
*I knew he would be late* (one future event) vs *Every day he would sit by the window* (past habit).
very soon vs at some point; *about to* is more imminent.
fixed arrangement (*I was meeting them at six*) vs intention (*I was going to meet them*).

blocks.text: *Was to* for destiny and *was to have done* for cancelled arrangements are formal and typical of historical narrative, biography and news. In conversation, *was going to* covers most cases.
Foreshadowing with *would* (*It would prove a costly mistake*) is a hallmark of narrative non-fiction and quality journalism; it creates suspense from hindsight.

rows.wrong: I knew she will pass the exam.
rows.right: I knew she would pass the exam.
rows.why: The viewpoint (*I knew*) is in the past, so *will* becomes *would*.

rows.wrong: I was going to call you, but I have forgotten.
rows.right: I was going to call you, but I forgot.
rows.why: The whole sequence is in the past: the plan and its failure both belong there.

rows.wrong: The concert was to held last week.
rows.right: The concert was to be held last week.
rows.why: *Was to* is followed by an infinitive; the passive infinitive is *be held*.

rows.wrong: We were about leaving when it started raining.
rows.right: We were about to leave when it started raining.
rows.why: *Be about* takes *to* + infinitive, not *-ing*.

rows.wrong: The bridge was to have open in 2020.
rows.right: The bridge was to have opened in 2020.
rows.why: *Was to have* + past participle describes a plan that did not happen.

rows.wrong: He said he is going to come, but he didn't.
rows.right: He said he was going to come, but he didn't.
rows.why: After a past reporting verb, *is going to* normally becomes *was going to*, especially when the plan failed.

blocks.text: Foreshadowing for rhetorical effect
*It **was to prove** a turning point.* *This decision **would come back** to haunt the government.* Narrative hindsight adds drama to historical or analytical writing.
Hedged reporting of plans
*The agreement **was due to** be signed in June* reports a schedule without asserting it happened; useful when the outcome is uncertain.
Combining with negative inversion
*Little **did** they realise that the project **would** take a decade.* *Never **was** the empire **to** regain its former power.*

items: Move a future form one step back to look forward from a past point: *will → would, am going to → was going to, am to → was to*.
*Was going to* and *was to have done* often signal plans that did not happen.
*Would* and *was to* in narrative reveal what happened later (foreshadowing).
*Was about to / on the point of* + *when* for interrupted imminent actions.
*Would have done* = completion before a future point seen from the past.

sentences.text: When Ada left school in 1998, she had no idea that she [[would]] one day run the national archive.
sentences.note: *would*: a later outcome seen from a past viewpoint

sentences.text: She started as a part-time cataloguer.
She [[was going to]] study law, but a summer job changed her mind.
sentences.note: *was going to*: a plan that was not carried out

sentences.text: Ten years later she [[was to]] become the youngest director in the archive's history.
sentences.note: *was to*: what lay ahead, in a formal narrative

sentences.text: Her colleagues remember her as patient and precise.
In 2020 she [[was about to]] announce a digitisation programme when the pandemic struck.
sentences.note: *was about to*: something on the point of happening

sentences.text: The programme finally launched two years later.

check.prompt: I ___ phone you last night, but I fell asleep.
check.explanation: A plan in the past that was not carried out: *was going to*.

check.prompt: Nobody suspected that the small start-up ___ a global brand.
check.explanation: The viewpoint is in the past (*nobody suspected*), so *will* becomes *would*.

check.prompt: Which sentence describes a plan that did NOT happen?
options: The new law was to come into force in May.
The new law was to have come into force in May.
The new law was going to come into force, and it did.
check.explanation: *Was to have* + past participle signals that the plan was not fulfilled.

check.prompt: Why might a historian write *He was to die in exile ten years later* rather than *He died in exile ten years later*?
check.model: *Was to* looks forward from the point reached in the story and presents the later event as what lay ahead for him; the past simple simply reports the fact.
check.explanation: This is a formal narrative use: the viewpoint stays in the story's past while revealing the future.

produce.prompt: Write 4–5 sentences about a turning point in someone's life, real or invented. Describe what they expected, what they planned and what was in fact to happen.
checklist: I used *would* for something expected or predicted from a past viewpoint.
I used *was going to* for a plan that did not happen, followed by what happened instead.
I used *was to* or *was about to* at least once.
My reporting verbs are in the past, and the forms after them have moved back correctly.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Habits: used to, would, be used to and will
summary: Several structures talk about typical behaviour. They differ in time (past or present), in whether they describe states or actions, and in the attitude of the speaker.

blocks.text: These forms all describe what is **typical**, but they look at habits from different angles. *Used to* and *would* look back at past habits that are no longer true. *Be used to* is completely different: it describes something that feels **normal and familiar** to you now.
*used to* + infinitive = a past habit or state, now finished · *would* + infinitive = a repeated past action (not a state) · *be/get used to* + *-ing* or a noun = be or become accustomed to.

items.en: I **used to** cycle to work.
items.note: I did it regularly; I don't any more.

items.en: I**'m used to** cycling in traffic.
items.note: It feels normal to me now.

blocks.text: Habitual forms describe things that happened regularly or were true for a long period. **used to** and **would** look back at past habits; **be/get used to** describes familiarity; **will** and **would** can describe typical (sometimes annoying) behaviour.

items.en: We **used to** live by the sea. Every summer we **would** swim before breakfast.

head: Structure
Form
Example
rows: didn't use to / Did you use to…?
*He **would** sit by the window for hours.*

blocks.text: In questions and negatives, *use to* has no *-d*: ~~Did you used to~~.

sections.title: Main rules: used to or would?

items: **used to** works for both **states and actions**: *I used to have long hair. I used to cycle to school.*
**would** works only for **repeated actions**, not states: ~~I would have long hair~~.
**would** normally needs a past time already established; it is common in nostalgic storytelling.
Use the **past simple** for a single past event or when you say how many times: *I went there twice*, not ~~I used to go there twice~~.

sections.title: be used to and get used to

blocks.text: These are completely different from *used to* + infinitive. They mean *be/become accustomed to* and are followed by a **noun or -ing form**:

items.en: She **isn't used to** driving on the left.
It took months to **get used to** the climate.
~~I'm used to get up early.~~
items.note: Use -ing: *I'm used to getting up early.*

sections.title: Typical and annoying behaviour: will, would, always + continuous

items: **will / would** (stressed in speech) for characteristic behaviour: *He'**ll** sit there for hours without saying a word.*
With stress, it shows irritation: *She **WOULD** say that!*
**always / constantly + continuous** for annoying habits: *You're always leaving the lights on!*

blocks.text: Habit markers (frequency adverbs, *every*, *whenever*) go with present simple or *used to/would* for the past. *These days* and *now* contrast present habits with past ones.

head: Expression
Example
rows: **in those days, back then, as a child**
**In those days** people **used to** write letters.
I **used to** smoke, but **these days** I **don't**.
She **no longer** works there. / She **doesn't** work there **any more**.

items.en: He's **always** borrowing my charger!

blocks.text: *Used to* and *would* need a past time frame. Don't use them with a specific number of times: ~~I used to visit Rome three times~~ → *I visited Rome three times.*

rows.wrong: I am used to live in a big city.
rows.right: I'm used to living in a big city. / I used to live in a big city.
rows.why: *Be used to* is followed by *-ing* (familiarity); *used to* + infinitive describes a past habit. Choose the meaning you need.

rows.wrong: I would have a dog when I was a child.
rows.right: I used to have a dog when I was a child.
rows.why: *Would* describes repeated actions, not states such as *have, live, be* or *believe*.

rows.wrong: I use to go to the gym.
rows.right: I usually go to the gym.
rows.why: *Used to* has no present form; for present habits use the present simple, often with an adverb.

rows.wrong: Did you used to live here?
rows.right: Did you use to live here?
rows.why: After *did* the verb is in the base form: *use to*.

rows.wrong: I can't get used to wake up early.
rows.right: I can't get used to waking up early.
rows.why: In *get used to*, *to* is a preposition, so it is followed by a noun or an *-ing* form.

blocks.text: In formal writing, prefer *formerly*, *traditionally*, *in the past* or *tended to*: *Families traditionally ate together*; *Earlier studies tended to overlook gender.* *Would* for past habit is more literary and narrative.

items: used to: past states and habits that are no longer true.
would: repeated past actions only, in narrative.
be/get used to + -ing: be/become familiar with.
will/would/always + continuous: characteristic or annoying behaviour.

sentences.text: When I was small, we [[used to]] spend every August at my grandmother's house.
sentences.note: *used to*: a past habit that has ended

sentences.text: Every morning she [[would]] wake us at six to collect the eggs.
sentences.note: *would*: a repeated past action in a nostalgic description

sentences.text: The house stood at the end of a dirt road.
There [[used to]] be a bakery opposite, but it closed years ago.
sentences.note: *used to* with a state: *would* is not possible here

sentences.text: Last year I went back for the first time.
I live in a city now, so I[['m not used to]] the silence at night any more.
sentences.note: *be used to* + noun: familiarity, not a past habit

sentences.text: It took me three nights to sleep properly.

check.prompt: When we were students, we ___ talk for hours in the café downstairs.
check.explanation: A repeated past action in a nostalgic description: *would* (or *used to*).

check.prompt: I ___ have long hair, but I cut it last year.
check.explanation: *Have* here is a state, so only *used to* is possible.

check.prompt: She's from Oslo, so she ___ cold winters.
check.explanation: *Be used to* + noun: the cold feels normal to her.

check.prompt: Explain the difference between *I used to drive on the left* and *I'm used to driving on the left*.
check.model: The first is a past habit that has ended: I don't drive on the left now. The second means that driving on the left feels normal and easy for me.
check.explanation: *Used to* + infinitive looks back; *be used to* + *-ing* describes present familiarity.

produce.prompt: Write 5–6 sentences comparing your life ten years ago with now. Describe past habits and states, and something you have had to get used to.
checklist: I used *used to* for at least one past state (for example *live, have, be*).
I used *would* only for repeated actions, not for states.
I used *be used to* or *get used to* followed by an *-ing* form or a noun.
My present habits are in the present simple, not *use to*.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Indirect questions and question tags
summary: Indirect questions make requests and enquiries more polite; question tags check information and invite agreement. Both depend on getting word order and auxiliaries exactly right.

blocks.text: Indirect questions and question tags both make communication **softer and more interactive**. An indirect question wraps a direct question inside a polite frame (*Could you tell me…?*). A question tag turns a statement into a check or an invitation to agree (*…, isn't it?*).
Indirect question: polite frame + statement word order, no *do/does/did*. Tag: positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag.

items.en: Where is the station? → **Could you tell me where the station is?**
items.note: statement word order inside the frame

items.en: You're from Kazan, **aren't you?**
You haven't seen my keys, **have you?**

blocks.text: **Indirect questions** sound more polite and less direct. **Question tags** are short questions at the end of a statement, used to check facts or invite the listener to agree.

items.en: **Could you tell me where the station is?**
items.note: more polite than *Where is the station?*

items.en: You're from Kazan, **aren't you?**
It's a lovely day, **isn't it?**

blocks.text: Indirect questions
After the introductory phrase, use **statement word order** (subject + verb) and no *do/does/did*.

head: Direct question
Indirect question
rows: Could you tell me where **the station is**?
Do you know what time **it opens**?
I'd like to know how much **it costs**.

blocks.text: Common introductions: *Could you tell me…? / Do you know…? / I was wondering… / Would you mind telling me…? / Have you any idea…? / I'd like to know…*
Yes/no questions need **if** or **whether**: *Do you know **if** the museum is open?*
Question tags
Positive statement → **negative tag**; negative statement → **positive tag**. Use the same auxiliary (or *do/does/did*) and a pronoun.

head: Statement
Tag
Note
rows: *nobody, nothing, never* are negative → positive tag

items: **Falling** intonation on a tag: you are fairly sure and expect agreement. *It's cold, ↘isn't it?*
**Rising** intonation: a real question; you're not sure. *You're coming, ↗aren't you?*
**Same-polarity tags** (positive + positive) show interest, surprise or sarcasm: *So you're the new manager, **are you**?*
Indirect questions are used for politeness, in formal emails and in interviews: *I was wondering whether you could send me the agenda.*

blocks.text: *I was wondering if…* and *Would you mind telling me…* are the most polite. *Any idea…?* is informal.

head: Indirect question (now, polite)
Reported question (telling what someone asked)
rows: Can you tell me if **it's** free?

blocks.text: Both use statement word order; reported questions usually also **backshift** the tense.

rows.wrong: Could you tell me where is the station?
rows.right: Could you tell me where the station is?
rows.why: Inside an indirect question, use statement word order.

rows.wrong: Do you know what time does the film start?
rows.right: Do you know what time the film starts?
rows.why: No *do/does/did* inside an indirect question.

rows.wrong: I wonder are they coming.
rows.right: I wonder if they're coming.
rows.why: A yes/no question needs *if* or *whether*.

rows.wrong: You haven't seen my keys, haven't you?
rows.right: You haven't seen my keys, have you?
rows.why: A negative statement takes a positive tag.

rows.wrong: I'm late, am not I?
rows.right: I'm late, aren't I?
rows.why: The standard tag for *I am* is *aren't I*.

items.en: **What** she said I can't remember.
items.note: A *wh*-clause as the object, fronted for emphasis.

items.en: It's anyone's guess **whether** the deal will go ahead.
**Whether** we like it or not, prices will rise.
items.note: *whether … or not* = it doesn't matter if

items.en: I'd be grateful if you could let me know **when** the results will be available.

blocks.text: In formal writing prefer *whether* to *if*, and always use *whether* after prepositions and before *to*-infinitives: *a debate about **whether** to ban cars* (~~about if~~).
Indirect questions: polite opener + (wh-word / if / whether) + **subject + verb**. Tags: opposite polarity, same auxiliary, pronoun subject.

items: *I'm…, aren't I? / Let's…, shall we? / Nobody…, did they?*
Falling tag = expecting agreement; rising tag = real question.

sentences.text: "Good evening. [[Could you tell me whether]] breakfast is included?"
"Yes, it's served from seven to ten."
"Great. The pool is on the top floor, [[isn't it]]?"
sentences.note: positive statement, negative tag: checking information

sentences.text: "[[Do you know what time]] the airport bus leaves?"
"You don't have a city map, [[do you]]?"
"Of course, here you are."

check.prompt: Could you tell me how much ___?
check.explanation: Indirect question: statement word order, no *does*.

check.prompt: She's never been to Paris, ___?
check.explanation: *Never* makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive.

check.prompt: Let's start, ___?
check.explanation: The tag after *Let's* is *shall we*.

check.prompt: How does intonation change the meaning of *It's Tuesday, isn't it?*
check.model: With falling intonation, the speaker is fairly sure and expects agreement. With rising intonation, the speaker is genuinely unsure and is asking a real question.
check.explanation: Tags can check information or invite agreement, depending on the tone.

produce.prompt: Write 5–6 lines you might use when arriving at a conference or a new workplace: polite questions to staff and small talk with another guest.
checklist: I used at least three indirect questions with statement word order.
I used *if* or *whether* for a yes/no indirect question.
I used at least two question tags, one after a positive and one after a negative statement.
I avoided *do/does/did* inside the indirect questions.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Emphasis: cleft sentences, inversion, fronting and auxiliary do
summary: English normally puts new or important information at the end of a sentence. Clefts, inversion, fronting and emphatic do let you control what the reader notices, which is essential for persuasive speaking and writing.

blocks.text: In a normal English sentence, the most important new information comes at the end. Emphasis structures change that order on purpose, to put **one part of the message in the spotlight**. Cleft sentences, inversion and fronting are tools for persuasion, contrast and drama.
Cleft: *It was X that…* / *What I need is…*. Inversion after a negative or limiting adverbial: *Never **have I** seen…*. Emphatic *do*: *I **do** understand.*

items.en: Maria solved the problem. → **It was Maria who** solved the problem.
items.note: the spotlight is on Maria, not someone else

items.en: I have never seen such a mess. → **Never have I seen** such a mess.
I need a long holiday. → **What I need is** a long holiday.
items.note: builds up to the key point

blocks.text: Emphasis structures change the normal order of information to highlight one part of the message. They are typical of persuasive essays, presentations and careful conversation.

head: Type
Pattern
Example
rows: ***It was the cost that** surprised me.*
***All I want is** a quiet weekend.*
***The reason (why) I left was** the pay.*

items.en: **It wasn't until** midnight **that** they finally agreed.
items.note: *It was not until…* = only at that time

blocks.text: Stressed *do/does/did* before the main verb contradicts or confirms strongly:

items.en: I **did** send the email, I promise!
She **does** work hard, even if it doesn't look like it.
**Do** sit down.

sections.title: Inversion after negative and limiting adverbials

blocks.text: When a negative or restrictive expression comes first, use **question word order** (auxiliary + subject):

head: Adverbial
Example
rows: ***Not only did** she win, **but** she **also** broke the record.*
***No sooner had** we arrived **than** it started to rain.*
Only then / Only after / Only when
***Only when** the results came **did we realise** our mistake.*
Under no circumstances / On no account
***Under no circumstances should you** share your password.*
***Little did they know** what was coming.*
***So severe was** the damage **that** the bridge closed.*

blocks.text: With *Only after / Only when / Not until*, invert the **main** clause, not the time clause: *Only when I got home **did I notice** the cut.*

items: **Fronting** moves an element to the start for contrast or emphasis: ***This** I cannot accept. **Strange** as it may seem, he was right.*
**Tailing** adds the topic at the end in speech: *It's lovely, **that beach**.* *He's very clever, **your brother**.*
**Concessive fronting**: *Much as I admire her, I disagree. Try as he might, he couldn't open it.*

items.en: I've never seen such chaos.
Never have I seen such chaos.
Jack broke the window.
It was Jack who broke the window.
What Jack did was break the window.

rows.wrong: Never I have seen such a mess.
rows.right: Never have I seen such a mess.
rows.why: After a fronted negative adverbial, the auxiliary comes before the subject, as in a question.

rows.wrong: Not only she sings, but she also dances.
rows.right: Not only does she sing, but she also dances.
rows.why: *Not only* at the start triggers inversion; with no auxiliary, add *do/does/did*.

rows.wrong: Only when I got home I noticed the cut.
rows.right: Only when I got home did I notice the cut.
rows.why: With *only when / only after*, the inversion is in the main clause.

rows.wrong: What I need it is a long holiday.
rows.right: What I need is a long holiday.
rows.why: In a *what*-cleft, the *what*-clause is the subject: no extra *it*.

rows.wrong: It was in 2019 when I moved here.
rows.right: It was in 2019 that I moved here.
rows.why: In *it*-clefts, use *that* after a time or place phrase (*when* is informal).

blocks.text: Inversion is formal and should be used sparingly in essays, typically once or twice for impact, especially in introductions and conclusions: *Not only does tourism create jobs, but it also funds conservation.* Clefts are useful in academic writing to signal contrast: *It is this assumption that the present study challenges.*

items: It-clefts and what-clefts move focus.
Emphatic *do* confirms or contradicts.
Negative/limiting adverbial first → auxiliary + subject.
Fronting and tailing for contrast and spoken style.

sentences.text: [[Never before have]] so many opportunities been open to people your age.
You have worked hard to get here.
[[What matters now is]] how you use what you have learned.
sentences.note: *what*-cleft: builds up to the key point

sentences.text: [[It was]] your curiosity, not your grades, [[that]] impressed us most.
[[Not only did]] you master the theory, but you also learned to work as a team.
We [[do]] believe that you will make a difference.

check.prompt: Rarely ___ such a talented student.
check.explanation: After *rarely* at the start, invert the auxiliary and subject.

check.prompt: ___ the noise that kept me awake, not the heat.
check.explanation: An *it*-cleft focuses on *the noise* in contrast to *the heat*.

check.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: No sooner I had arrived than it started raining.
No sooner had I arrived than it started raining.
No sooner had I arrived when it started raining.
check.explanation: *No sooner* + inversion, followed by *than*.

check.prompt: Why might a speaker say *What we need is more time* instead of *We need more time*?
check.model: The *what*-cleft delays the key information (*more time*) to the end, where it gets the most emphasis; it sounds more deliberate and persuasive.
check.explanation: Clefts control where the spotlight falls.

produce.prompt: Write a short persuasive paragraph (5–6 sentences) arguing for a change in your town, school or workplace. Use emphasis to highlight your main points.
checklist: I used at least one *it*-cleft and one *what*-cleft.
I used inversion after a negative or limiting adverbial (*never, rarely, not only, only when*).
I used emphatic *do / does / did* once.
Every inversion has the auxiliary before the subject.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Linking ideas: contrast, concession, cause and result
summary: Linkers show the logical relationship between ideas. Using the right one, with the right grammar after it, is essential for coherent essays and arguments.

blocks.text: Linkers show the **logical relationship** between ideas: contrast, concession, cause, result or addition. Choosing the right meaning is only half the job; each linker also belongs to a grammatical type that decides **what comes after it**: a clause, a noun phrase, or a new sentence.
Conjunctions (*although, because, whereas*) + clause. Prepositions (*despite, because of, due to*) + noun or *-ing*. Adverbs (*however, therefore, moreover*) link sentences: *…grew. However, …*

items.en: **Although** it was raining, we went out.
**Despite** the rain, we went out.
It was raining. **However**, we went out.
items.note: adverb at the start of a new sentence

blocks.text: Linking devices connect clauses and sentences: contrast (*however*), concession (*although*), cause (*because of*), result (*therefore*), addition (*moreover*). Each belongs to a grammatical type, which decides what follows it.

head: Type
Followed by
Examples
rows: *although, even though, while, whereas, because, so*
*despite, in spite of, because of, due to, owing to*
a new sentence (often after a full stop or semicolon)

items.en: **Although** it was raining, we went out.
**Despite** the rain / **Despite** it raining, we went out.
It was raining. **However**, we went out.

items: **while / whereas** contrast two facts: *The north is wet, **whereas** the south is dry.*
**although / even though / though** concede a point: ***Even though** he was ill, he finished the race.* (*even though* is stronger)
**despite / in spite of** + noun / -ing / *the fact that*: ***Despite the fact that** prices rose, sales increased.*
**however / nevertheless / nonetheless / even so** start a new sentence.
**Adverbials of concession** (C1): *admittedly, granted, all the same, be that as it may*.

head: Cause
Result
rows: so, so … that, such … that (+ clause)
because of, due to, owing to, as a result of (+ noun)
therefore, consequently, as a result, thus, hence (sentence adverbs)

items.en: The match was cancelled **due to** heavy rain.
The rain was heavy. **Consequently**, the match was cancelled.

blocks.text: *Due to* traditionally follows *be*: *The delay was due to fog.* In formal writing, prefer *owing to / because of* at the start of a sentence.
*Moreover, Furthermore, In addition, What is more, Besides* add points; *provided that, as long as, unless* add conditions (see *Conditionals*).

items.en: Although it was late, …
~~Although of the late hour, …~~
On the other hand…
items.note: introduces the other side of an argument

items.en: On the contrary…
items.note: says the previous idea is false: *It wasn't boring. On the contrary, it was fascinating.*

rows.wrong: Despite of the weather, we went.
rows.right: Despite the weather, we went. / In spite of the weather, we went.
rows.why: *Despite* has no *of*; *in spite of* has one.

rows.wrong: Although he was tired, but he continued.
rows.right: Although he was tired, he continued.
rows.why: Use one linker for one relationship, not two.

rows.wrong: The economy grew, however unemployment rose.
rows.right: The economy grew; however, unemployment rose.
rows.why: *However* is an adverb: it starts a new sentence or follows a semicolon.

rows.wrong: Because of it was late, we took a taxi.
rows.right: Because it was late, we took a taxi. / Because of the late hour, we took a taxi.
rows.why: *Because* + clause; *because of* + noun.

rows.wrong: Despite he was ill, he went to work.
rows.right: Despite being ill, he went to work. / Although he was ill, he went to work.
rows.why: *Despite* cannot be followed by a full clause.

items: Fronted concession: ***Much as** I admire the plan, it is unrealistic.* ***Difficult though** it may be, we must act.*
*Whereas* and *while* can begin the sentence for balanced contrast.
Overusing *Moreover/Furthermore* at the start of every sentence sounds mechanical; vary with *This also…, A further problem is…*.

blocks.text: Formal: *nevertheless, consequently, thus, hence, notwithstanding*. Neutral: *however, therefore, although*. Informal: *but, so, anyway, still*. Good essays use a range, placed naturally, and not at the start of every sentence.

items: Conjunction + clause; preposition + noun/-ing; sentence adverb + new sentence.
*although/even though* vs *despite/in spite of*.
*because* + clause vs *because of/due to* + noun.
*on the other hand* (other side) vs *on the contrary* (rejecting).

recognise.title: A short report on remote work

sentences.text: [[Although]] remote work saves commuting time, it can increase isolation.
Productivity rose in the first year. [[However]], it fell slightly in the second.
[[Due to]] these mixed results, the company is reviewing its policy.
Staff will be consulted in May.
Some teams prefer the office, [[whereas]] others want full flexibility.
[[Despite]] the challenges, most employees support hybrid working.

check.prompt: ___ the high price, the tickets sold out in an hour.
check.explanation: *Despite* + noun phrase.

check.prompt: The plan was expensive. ___, it was approved.
check.explanation: A sentence adverb linking two sentences.

check.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: Because of the train was late, I missed the meeting.
Because the train was late, I missed the meeting.
Because the train late, I missed the meeting.
check.explanation: *Because* + full clause.

check.prompt: What is the difference in grammar between *although* and *however*?
check.model: *Although* is a conjunction that joins a subordinate clause to a main clause in one sentence. *However* is an adverb that links two separate sentences (or clauses after a semicolon).
check.explanation: The grammatical type decides the punctuation and what follows.

produce.prompt: Write a short balanced paragraph (5–6 sentences) about the advantages and disadvantages of a technology you use every day.
checklist: I used a conjunction (*although, whereas, while*) + clause.
I used a preposition (*despite, due to, because of*) + noun or *-ing*.
I used a sentence adverb (*however, therefore, moreover*) with correct punctuation.
I used only one linker for each relationship.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Modals: obligation, deduction and stance
summary: Modal verbs and modal expressions show how certain, necessary or permitted something is. At C1, modality also means signalling your stance with adjectives, adverbs and nouns.

blocks.text: Modal verbs show the speaker's **attitude** to an action or a statement. They answer two kinds of question. *Is it necessary, allowed or advisable?* That is obligation and permission. *How sure am I that it's true?* That is deduction and probability. The same verb, especially *must*, can do both jobs.
Obligation: *must, have to, should, can, needn't*. Certainty: *must* (I'm sure it is) → *should, will* → *may, might, could* → *can't* (I'm sure it isn't).

items.en: You **must** wear a helmet.
She **must** be tired after the flight.
She **must have** left already.
items.note: deduction about the past: *modal* + *have* + past participle

blocks.text: Modality expresses the speaker's attitude to a statement. Two main areas:

items: **Obligation and permission** (deontic): *must, have to, should, can, be allowed to, needn't*.
**Probability and deduction** (epistemic): *must, can't, might, could, may, should, will*.

blocks.text: Modal verbs (*can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would*) take a bare infinitive, have no *-s* and form questions by inversion. Semi-modals (*have to, need to, be able to, ought to, be supposed to*) behave more like normal verbs.

head: Meaning
Forms
rows: *don't have to, needn't, don't need to*
*mustn't, can't, aren't allowed to, be forbidden to*
*can, may (formal), be allowed to, be permitted to*

items.en: You **mustn't** smoke here.
You **don't have to** come.
We **didn't need to** pay.
items.note: it wasn't necessary (we probably didn't pay)

items.en: We **needn't have paid**.
items.note: we paid, but it wasn't necessary

items.en: She's not answering. She **must be** in a meeting.
He **can't have taken** the train; there were no trains that night.

blocks.text: The negative of deductive *must* is *can't*, not ~~mustn't~~: *That can't be right.*

items.en: You **should have told** me.
You **could have told** me.
items.note: reproach: it was possible but you didn't

items.en: **Could** you swim when you were five?
I **managed to / was able to** escape.
You **had better** leave now.
items.note: strong advice with a warning; refers to now or the future

sections.title: Advanced usage: modality beyond modal verbs

blocks.text: At C1 you can express the same meanings more precisely with other structures:

items: adjectives: *It is **highly unlikely** that…*, *It is **essential** that…*, *X is **bound/liable/apt** to…*
adverbs: *conceivably, presumably, inevitably, arguably*
nouns: *There is **every likelihood** that…*, *There's **no question of**…*, *in all probability*
verbs: *It **remains to be seen** whether…*, *The data **suggest** that…*

items.en: **In all likelihood**, the trial will be postponed.
It is **imperative** that every passenger **wear** a seat belt.

rows.wrong: You mustn't to wear a tie.
rows.right: You don't have to wear a tie.
rows.why: Modals are followed by the infinitive without *to*. And *mustn't* means "it is forbidden"; *don't have to* means "it isn't necessary".

rows.wrong: He must have been at home yesterday, I'm not sure.
rows.right: He might have been at home yesterday.
rows.why: *Must have* expresses near-certainty; if you are unsure, use *might have* or *may have*.

rows.wrong: I could finish the marathon last year.
rows.right: I managed to finish the marathon last year.
rows.why: For one specific achievement in the past, use *managed to* or *was able to*, not *could*.

rows.wrong: She can't to come tomorrow.
rows.right: She can't come tomorrow.
rows.why: No *to* after a modal verb.

rows.wrong: You needn't to worry.
rows.right: You needn't worry. / You don't need to worry.
rows.why: Modal *needn't* takes a bare infinitive; *need* as a main verb takes *to*.

blocks.text: Academic writing uses modality to **hedge** claims: *These findings **may** indicate…*, *This **could** be explained by…*, *It **would seem** that…*. Strong modals (*must, certainly*) are reserved for well-supported claims. Formal rules use *be required to, be prohibited from, be permitted to*.

items: Obligation: must/have to; no obligation: don't have to/needn't; prohibition: mustn't.
Deduction: must (sure), can't (sure not), might/could (possible); past = modal + have + V3.
*needn't have done* = did it unnecessarily; *didn't need to do* = it wasn't necessary.
At C1, use adjectives, adverbs and nouns of likelihood to state your stance precisely.

sentences.text: All students [[must]] bring a waterproof jacket.
You [[don't have to]] buy special boots; trainers are fine.
The coach leaves at eight.
It [[might]] rain in the afternoon, so pack an umbrella.
The guide [[must have]] walked this route a hundred times; she knows every stone.
Lunch is included in the price.
You [[shouldn't]] leave food on the trail.

check.prompt: "Is that Anna's car?" "It ___ be hers: she sold her car last month."
check.explanation: *Can't* expresses certainty that something is not true.

check.prompt: You ___ pay now: you can pay at the end of the month.
check.explanation: No obligation: *don't have to*. *Mustn't* would mean it is forbidden.

check.prompt: The lights are off. They ___ gone to bed.
check.explanation: A confident deduction about the past: *must have* + past participle.

check.prompt: Explain the difference between *You mustn't tell her* and *You don't have to tell her*.
check.model: *You mustn't tell her* means it is forbidden: don't tell her. *You don't have to tell her* means it is not necessary, but you can if you want.
check.explanation: Negative *must* and negative *have to* have different meanings.

produce.prompt: Write 5–6 sentences of advice for someone starting a new job in your field. Include rules, things that are not necessary, and at least two guesses about the situation or about the past.
checklist: I used *must* or *have to* for obligation and *don't have to* for no obligation.
I used *should* or *ought to* for advice.
I used *might*, *must* or *can't* for at least one deduction.
I used a past deduction (*must have / might have / can't have* + past participle).

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Multi-word verbs: phrasal and prepositional verbs, word order and register
summary: "Look up a word" and "look at a word" look alike but behave differently. Knowing the grammar of multi-word verbs lets you place objects correctly, form passives and nouns, and choose between a phrasal verb and a formal single-word verb.

blocks.text: Multi-word verbs combine a verb with one or two particles: *give up, look into, put up with*. Their meaning is often not the sum of the parts, and their **grammar depends on the type**: whether the particle is an adverb (separable) or a preposition (not separable).
Separable phrasal verbs: the object can go before or after the particle, but a pronoun must go in the middle: *turn **it** off*. Prepositional verbs: the object always follows: *look **after** her*.

items.en: Turn off the light. / Turn the light off. / Turn **it** off.
items.note: separable: a pronoun goes in the middle

items.en: She looks after her grandmother. / She looks after **her**.
I can't put up with this noise.

blocks.text: English has thousands of verbs made of a verb plus a particle: *give up, look into, put up with, carry out*. They are not one category but three, and their grammar differs: where the object can go, whether the particle is stressed, and whether they can be passivised. Advanced users also need to know when a phrasal verb is the natural choice and when a formal equivalent is better.

sections.title: How it works: adverb particles and prepositions

blocks.text: The particle after the verb is either an **adverb** (*up, out, away, back, down, off*) or a **preposition** (*at, for, into, with, on*).

items: **Phrasal verbs** (verb + adverb particle): the particle belongs to the verb and changes its meaning: *give up* (stop), *turn down* (refuse). The particle can usually move: *turn down **the offer** / turn **the offer** down*.
**Prepositional verbs** (verb + preposition): the preposition belongs to the object noun phrase: *look **at the chart**, rely **on volunteers***. The object always follows the preposition.
**Phrasal-prepositional verbs** (verb + adverb + preposition): *put up **with**, look forward **to**, come up **with**, get away **with***. The object follows the whole sequence.

blocks.text: A pronoun object goes **between** the verb and the adverb particle of a phrasal verb: *turn **it** down* (~~turn down it~~), but **after** the preposition of a prepositional verb: *look **at it***.

head: Type
Object position
Example
Passive
rows: before or after particle; pronoun before

blocks.text: Stress
Adverb particles are usually stressed: *She turned it **DOWN**.* Prepositions are usually unstressed: *She **LOOKED** at it.*
Long objects
With a long object, put the particle first: *They turned **down** every proposal that the committee had submitted* (not *turned every proposal ... down*).
1. Literal, aspectual and idiomatic meaning

items: **Literal**: *take the boxes **out***.
**Aspectual** (the particle adds completion, continuation or beginning): *eat **up**, use **up*** (completely); *carry **on**, keep **on*** (continue); *set **off**, start **up*** (begin).
**Idiomatic**: *put off* (postpone), *come across* (find by chance), *bring about* (cause).

blocks.text: 2. Nouns and adjectives from phrasal verbs

*break down → a breakdown; turn out → the turnout; set back → a setback; cut back → cutbacks; drop out → a dropout; outcome, outbreak, input, upkeep, follow-up, built-up area, worn-out shoes.* These nouns are common even in formal writing.
3. Register choice

Many phrasal verbs have a Latinate equivalent: *find out / discover, put off / postpone, set up / establish, look into / investigate, carry out / conduct, go up / increase, point out / indicate.* Phrasal verbs are natural in speech and most journalism; academic writing often prefers the single verb, but some phrasal verbs are fully academic: *carry out, point out, set out, account for, rule out, draw on, bring about*.

items.en: The researchers **carried out** a series of interviews.
items.note: academic phrasal verb, natural in formal writing

items.en: We need to **rule out** other explanations before drawing conclusions.
I **came across** an interesting article; I'll send it **over**.
The proposal was **turned down** because it was too expensive.
items.note: passive of a separable phrasal verb

items.en: You shouldn't **put up with** that kind of behaviour.
The strike led to a major **setback** for the negotiations.
The decline **can be accounted for** by changes in demand.
items.note: passive prepositional verb in academic style

head: Pair
Difference
rows: *look up a word* vs *look up the street*
phrasal (search for: *look it up*) vs verb + prepositional phrase (direction: *look up it* is impossible; *look up the street* = towards).
prepositional (visit / formally ask: *call on someone*) vs phrasal (phone; summon: *call someone up*).
same meaning; *turn down* is neutral/informal, *refuse/decline* more formal.
*get over* an illness or disappointment (recover); *overcome* a difficulty (formal, effort).
invent (*make up a story*), constitute (*women make up 60%*), reconcile (*they made up*), compensate (*make up for lost time*). Context decides.

blocks.text: Informal phrasal verbs such as *get on with, mess up, sort out, chuck out* belong in speech and informal writing. In essays, prefer *proceed, spoil, resolve, discard* — but do not replace academic phrasal verbs like *carry out, point out, account for* with odd formal equivalents.
Overly formal single verbs in conversation sound stiff: *We must postpone the meeting* is fine at work, but among friends *Let's put it off* is more natural.

rows.wrong: I looked up it in the dictionary.
rows.right: I looked it up in the dictionary.
rows.why: With a separable phrasal verb, a pronoun object goes between the verb and the particle.

rows.wrong: Can you pick up me at eight?
rows.right: Can you pick me up at eight?

rows.wrong: They called off it because of the rain.
rows.right: They called it off because of the rain.
rows.why: Pronoun object in the middle.

rows.wrong: She is looking forward to meet you.
rows.right: She is looking forward to meeting you.
rows.why: *To* is a preposition, so it is followed by *-ing*.

rows.wrong: I'll look her after this weekend.
rows.right: I'll look after her this weekend.
rows.why: *Look after* is a prepositional verb: the object always follows the preposition.

blocks.text: Particles with consistent meanings

Learning particle meanings speeds up acquisition: **up** = completion or increase (*fill up, step up, scale up*); **down** = reduction or recording (*scale down, write down, narrow down*); **out** = to the end or outward (*sort out, wear out, phase out*); **off** = separation or cancellation (*call off, cut off, write off*); **through** = to completion (*follow through, see through*).
Academic phrasal verbs worth mastering
*account for, bear out, build on, carry out, draw on, embark on, factor in, point out, rule out, set out, single out, spell out, stem from, weigh up.*
Particle placement for emphasis
In speech the object can follow the particle for end-focus even if short: *He gave back **the money** — all of it.* But with pronouns, separation remains obligatory.

items: Phrasal verbs: verb + adverb particle; object can separate; pronouns go in the middle.
Prepositional verbs: verb + preposition; object always after the preposition.
Phrasal-prepositional verbs: object after both particles (*put up with it*).
Many phrasal verbs form nouns (*setback, outcome, breakdown*).
Choose register carefully: some phrasal verbs are academic, others are informal.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Narrative tenses and the past perfect
summary: Telling a story in English means choosing between past simple, past continuous, past perfect and past perfect continuous to show order, background and cause.

blocks.text: When you tell a story, each past tense has a different job. The **past simple** moves the story forward, event by event. The **past continuous** paints the background: what was going on around those events. The **past perfect** steps back to something that had already happened before them.
Main events → past simple. Background → past continuous. An earlier event → past perfect.

items.en: The lights **were flickering** when I **got** home. Someone **had left** the door open.
items.note: background → main event → an earlier event that explains it

blocks.text: The past perfect is a tool for going *back*, not a "more past" tense: you need it only when the order of events would otherwise be unclear, or when you want to stress that something happened first.

Narrative tenses organise a story in time. The **past simple** moves the story forward; the **past continuous** describes the background; the **past perfect** steps back to an earlier event; the **past perfect continuous** shows an activity that continued up to a past moment.

items.en: It **was raining** and the streets **were** empty. I **had been walking** for an hour when I **realised** I **had left** my keys at the office.

head: Tense
Form
Function in a story
rows: duration up to a past moment, causes

items: Use the **past perfect** only when you need to make the earlier time clear. If events are told in order, the past simple is enough: *I got up, had a shower and left.*
Use it after **time conjunctions** when the order matters: *When I arrived, the film started* (I arrived, then it started) vs *When I arrived, the film had started* (it started before).
With **before, after, as soon as**, the past perfect is optional because the conjunction already shows the order.
Use the **past perfect continuous** to explain a visible result in the past: *Her eyes were red: she had been crying.*

blocks.text: Linkers show the order of events; the tense shows how the speaker sees them. Choose the linker first, then check the tense.

head: Expression
Typical tense
Example
rows: **While** we **were packing**, the lights went out.
**By the time** we arrived, the film **had started**.
**for, since** (looking back from a past point)
**then, next, eventually, in the end, at last**

items.en: **No sooner had** we sat down **than** the phone rang.
items.note: Inverted pattern for emphasis — see *Inversion and emphasis*.

items.en: **Hardly** had she arrived **when** the trouble began.

blocks.text: *After* and *before* already show order, so the past perfect is optional: *After she (had) left, I called him.*

items.en: When she came in, we **had** dinner.
items.note: She came in, then we ate.

items.en: When she came in, we **were having** dinner.
items.note: We were in the middle of dinner.

items.en: When she came in, we **had had** dinner.
I **had read** the book twice.
I **had been reading** for hours.

sections.title: Other ways to talk about the past

items: **used to / would** for past habits (see *Habits: used to and would*).
**was going to / was about to** for plans that did not happen: *I was going to call you, but I forgot.*
**The historic present**: storytellers and journalists sometimes use present tenses to make a past story vivid: *So I'm walking home, and this man stops me…* (informal speech, C1).

rows.wrong: After I had finished, I had gone home.
rows.right: After I had finished, I went home.
rows.why: Only the earlier event needs the past perfect; the main event stays in the past simple.

rows.wrong: Yesterday I had met an old friend.
rows.right: Yesterday I met an old friend.
rows.why: There is no earlier past event to refer back to, so the past simple is enough.

rows.wrong: I was knowing the answer.
rows.right: I knew the answer.
rows.why: *Know* is a state verb and is not normally used in the continuous.

rows.wrong: I didn't recognise him at first. I never met him before.
rows.right: I didn't recognise him at first. I had never met him before.
rows.why: *Never… before* looks back from a past moment over the time up to it, which needs the past perfect.

rows.wrong: While I walked home, it was starting to rain.
rows.right: While I was walking home, it started to rain.
rows.why: The longer background action takes the continuous; the short event that interrupts it takes the past simple.

items: Writers use the past perfect for **flashbacks**, then return to the past simple once the earlier time is established, to avoid a long chain of *had*.
**Hardly / No sooner** with the past perfect and inversion (formal): *No sooner had we sat down than the alarm went off.* (See *Inversion and emphasis*.)
**Perfect infinitives** for reported past: *He is said to have left the country.*

blocks.text: In historical and academic narratives, the past perfect frames background before the main period: *By 1900, the city's population had doubled.* Avoid the historic present in formal essays unless you are summarising a literary plot, where the present simple is standard: *In the novel, the protagonist returns home…*

items: Past simple moves the story; continuous gives background; perfect steps back.
Use the past perfect only where order would otherwise be unclear.
Past perfect continuous explains causes and duration up to a past point.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Negation, scope and focusing adverbs: not, no, hardly, only, even
summary: Where you put "not" or "only" decides what you are denying or highlighting. Advanced English uses negative transfer, negative quantifiers and understatement to make claims precise and tactful.

blocks.text: A negative or focusing word does not affect the whole sentence equally; it applies to a particular part of it, called its **scope**. Moving *not*, *only* or *even* can change what you are claiming. Advanced English also follows conventions for negating politely, such as *I don't think…* rather than *I think… not*.
Put *not, only, even* as close as possible to the part you want to negate or focus on. Negate the opinion verb, not the clause: *I don't think it's fair*.

items.en: **Not all** the students passed.
**Only** Maria passed the test.
Maria **only** passed the test.
items.note: she passed, but only just, or did nothing more

blocks.text: *All the students didn't pass* and *Not all the students passed* look similar but can mean different things. *I don't think it's fair* is more natural than *I think it isn't fair*. *Only* in different positions changes the claim. This lesson is about **what** a negative or focusing word applies to — its **scope** — and the conventions English uses to negate politely and precisely.

sections.title: How it works: scope and focus

blocks.text: A negative or focusing word affects the part of the sentence that follows it and falls within its **scope**. Compare:

items.en: She **deliberately didn't** answer.
She **didn't deliberately** answer.

blocks.text: In speech, stress marks the focus: *I didn't say she **stole** the money* (I said something else about the money) vs *I didn't say **she** stole the money* (someone else did). In writing, there is no stress, so **word order** and **choice of structure** must make the scope clear.
Put a negative or focusing word as close as possible to the element it applies to. When in doubt, restructure: *Not all of the data were usable* is clearer than *All of the data weren't usable*.
Negative forms

head: Form
Example
Note
rows: *We don't have **any** data. I didn't go **either**.*
***None of** the samples was / were contaminated.*
***Neither** option is ideal. She didn't agree, **nor** did I.*
one negative per clause in standard English
negative meaning; take positive tags: *..., do we?*
negative: "not much/many" (*a little, a few* are positive)

blocks.text: Focusing adverbs

head: Adverb
Position and meaning
rows: before the focused element in writing: *We **only** tested **adults*** (ambiguous) → *We tested **only adults*** (precise)
adds surprise: ***Even** experts disagree. They didn't **even** reply.*
= only/exactly: *It's **just** a theory. That's **just** what I meant.*
restrict to a subset: *The effect was strong, **particularly among** older users.*

blocks.text: 1. Negative transfer (raising)

With *think, believe, suppose, expect, imagine, seem, appear*, English normally negates the main verb, not the clause: *I **don't think** he's right* (not *I think he isn't right*), *It **doesn't seem** likely.* This sounds less direct and more polite.
2. Partial versus total negation
***Not all** respondents agreed* = some did not. ***No** respondents agreed / **None** of the respondents agreed* = zero agreement. *All respondents didn't agree* is ambiguous; avoid it in writing.
3. Understatement (litotes)

Negating a negative adjective gives a cautious positive: *not uncommon* (fairly common), *not unreasonable*, *not insignificant*, *not without problems*. Very common in academic and diplomatic English.
4. Negative tags and responses
After negative adverbs, use positive tags: *She **seldom** complains, **does** she?* Responses agree with the negative: *"I can't swim." "**Neither** can I." / "Nor can I." / "Me neither."*

items.en: I **don't believe** the figures have been checked.
**Not every** policy that sounds fair is fair in practice.
There is **little** evidence to support this claim.
The results are **not insignificant**.
items.note: litotes: cautious way to say *quite significant*

items.en: **Only** later did the team realise the error.
The change affected **only** part-time staff.
He **didn't even** apologise.
items.note: *even* stresses that the minimum expected action was missing

head: Pair
Difference
rows: negative (*little time* = not enough) vs positive (*a little time* = some). Same for *few / a few*.
*no* + noun is more emphatic: *It's **no** surprise* vs *It's **not a** surprise*. *Not* before adjectives: *not easy*.
*I didn't see anyone* = *I saw no one* (formal). Never *~~I didn't see no one~~* in standard English.
*hardly* = almost not; *hard* = with effort. *Hardly any/ever* = almost none/never.
positive addition *also/too*; negative addition *either*: *I don't like it **either*** (~~too~~).

blocks.text: Formal: *no, none, neither, nor, scarcely, seldom, little, few*. Neutral/informal: *not any, not ... either, hardly, me neither*. Double negatives (*I don't know nothing*) are features of some dialects and informal speech, but non-standard in writing.
Litotes and negative transfer are key politeness devices in British English: *That's **not the best** idea* often means *That's a bad idea*. Be aware of this when interpreting feedback.

rows.wrong: I think it isn't a good idea.
rows.right: I don't think it's a good idea.
rows.why: English normally negates the opinion verb (*think, believe, expect*), not the clause after it.

rows.wrong: All the students didn't pass the exam. (meaning some failed)
rows.right: Not all the students passed the exam.
rows.why: *Not all* makes the scope clear: some passed, some didn't.

rows.wrong: I don't like coffee too.
rows.right: I don't like coffee either.
rows.why: In negative sentences, *too* becomes *either*.

rows.wrong: He hardly didn't sleep.
rows.right: He hardly slept.
rows.why: *Hardly* is already negative; do not add *not*.

rows.wrong: None of us have no idea.
rows.right: None of us has any idea. / None of us have any idea.
rows.why: One negative is enough; after a negative, use *any*.

rows.wrong: Few people came, so it was crowded.
rows.right: Few people came, so it was quiet.
rows.why: *Few* means "not many" (a negative idea); *a few* means "some".

blocks.text: Negative inversion for rhetoric
***Under no circumstances** should the data be shared. **Not only** was it late, it was incomplete. **At no point** did the minister apologise.* (See the inversion lesson.)
Scope in academic claims

*This does **not necessarily** mean ...* / *This **necessarily does not** mean ...*: the first denies necessity (it may or may not mean it); the second asserts a necessary negative. Precision here matters in argument.
Focusing adverbs with numbers
*The scheme reached **just** 12% of eligible households* (= a disappointingly small number) vs *as many as 12%* (= surprisingly large). The adverb carries the writer's evaluation.

items: Place *not, only, even* close to what they affect; restructure to avoid ambiguous scope.
Prefer negative transfer: *I don't think X* rather than *I think not-X*.
*Not all* = partial; *no/none* = total.
*Little/few* are negative, *a little/a few* positive.
Use litotes (*not uncommon*) for cautious claims; use positive tags after *hardly, seldom*.

sentences.text: [[I don't think]] the introduction is long enough.
[[Not all]] of your sources are recent.
Your conclusion is clear and well argued.
You have [[hardly]] mentioned the counter-arguments.
[[Only]] the second section needs major changes.
[[Even]] the tables are well formatted.

check.explanation: *Not all* clearly limits the negation to part of the group.

check.prompt: "I can't swim." "I can't ___."
check.explanation: *Either* in negative agreement.

check.prompt: There's ___ milk left; we need to buy some.
check.explanation: *Hardly* + *any*: one negative only.

check.model: *Only I saw the film* means nobody else saw it. *I only saw the film* means that seeing it is all I did (I didn't read the book, for example), or that I saw only that film.
check.explanation: The position of *only* changes what it focuses on.
