author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Noun clauses: that-clauses, wh-clauses and whether
summary: A noun clause does the job of a noun: it can be the subject, object or complement of a sentence. Noun clauses let you package whole ideas, which is essential for argument and academic writing.

blocks.text: A noun clause is a whole clause that does the job of a **noun**: it can be the subject or object of a sentence. It lets you treat a statement, a question or a fact as a single "thing" you can talk about: *I understand **why the system failed***.
Statement → *that*-clause (*I know **that** she's right*). Question → *wh*-clause or *whether/if*, with **statement word order** (*I wonder **where she lives***).

items.en: **What the data show** is that the effect is temporary.
We don't know **whether the plan will work**.
items.note: a yes/no question turned into a noun clause

blocks.text: Compare *I understand **the problem*** with *I understand **why the system failed***. The clause *why the system failed* fills the same position as the noun phrase *the problem*. That is a **noun clause** (also called a nominal or content clause). Noun clauses let you treat a statement, a question or a fact as a single unit you can then describe, evaluate or argue about: ***What the data show** is **that** the effect is temporary.*

sections.title: How it works: three families of noun clause

blocks.text: 1. **That-clauses** package a statement: *(that) the experiment worked*. 2. **Wh-clauses** package an open question or an unknown: *what happened, why prices rose, how the scheme works*. 3. **Whether/if-clauses** package a yes/no question: *whether the policy is fair*. Because they are no longer real questions, wh- and whether-clauses use **statement word order**: *I wonder why **she left*** (not *~~why did she leave~~*). This is the same logic as indirect questions.

Noun clauses can stand where nouns stand: **subject** (*That he resigned surprised everyone*), **object** (*I doubt whether it matters*), **complement** (*The problem is that we lack data*), **after a preposition** (*It depends on **what** you mean*) and **in apposition** to a noun (*the fact **that** he lied*).

head: Position
That-clause
Wh-clause
Whether-clause
rows: ***Whether** it works* remains to be seen.
The question is **whether** we can afford it.
It depends on **how** you do it.

blocks.text: *That* can be omitted after common reporting verbs and adjectives in informal style (*I think you're right*), but not when the clause is the subject (***That** he lied is obvious*).
1. Packaging an idea as the topic

Starting with a noun clause puts the idea in focus: ***How** universities should be funded** is a recurring debate.* Long subject clauses are often moved to the end with anticipatory *it* (see that lesson): *It is unclear **whether** the scheme works.*
2. Reporting and evaluating

Reporting verbs (*argue, claim, suggest, demonstrate*) take that-clauses; verbs of uncertainty (*wonder, ask, doubt, investigate, establish*) take wh- or whether-clauses: *The study investigates **whether** sleep affects recall.*
3. Talking about facts with prepositions

Prepositions cannot be followed directly by a that-clause. Use ***the fact that***: *Despite **the fact that** it rained, ...*; *She was annoyed **by the fact that** nobody replied.* (Or rephrase: *Although it rained ...*)
4. Nominal relative clauses
*What, whatever, whoever, wherever* create clauses meaning "the thing(s) that / anyone who": *I'll do **whatever** it takes.* These are covered in detail in the lesson on nominal relative clauses.

items.en: **That** the climate is changing is no longer disputed.
It is no longer disputed **that** the climate is changing.
The report does not explain **how** the figures were calculated.
Much depends on **whether** the government acts quickly.
items.note: whether-clause after a preposition (*if* is not possible here)

items.en: The assumption **that** growth is always good needs examining.
I'm not convinced **(that)** this is the right approach.
**Why** some languages die out while others thrive is a complex question.

head: Pair
Difference
rows: *the news **that** she had won* (= content of the news; *that* cannot be replaced by *which*) vs *the news **that/which** she brought* (relative: *that* is the object of *brought*).

Both introduce yes/no clauses after verbs (*I don't know whether/if ...*). Only *whether* is possible: as subject, after prepositions, before *to*-infinitive (*whether to go*) and with *or not* immediately after (*whether or not*).
*what* = the thing which: *What he said was true.* *That* introduces a fact: *That he said it was true* (= the fact of his saying it).
*Do you know where **she lives**?* not *~~where does she live~~*.
After prepositions and as a heavy subject, *the fact that* is required or clearer.

blocks.text: Subject that-clauses (*That X is true is clear*) are formal and can sound heavy; most writers prefer *It is clear that X*. Subject wh-clauses (*What matters is ...*) are common in both speech and writing as a focusing device.
Overuse of *the fact that* makes prose wordy: *Due to the fact that* → *because*; *In spite of the fact that* → *although*. Keep it where a noun phrase is genuinely needed.

rows.wrong: I don't know what does he want.
rows.right: I don't know what he wants.
rows.why: Noun clauses use statement word order, with no *do/does/did*.

rows.wrong: Despite that it was late, we continued.
rows.right: Despite the fact that it was late, we continued. / Although it was late, we continued.
rows.why: *Despite* is a preposition; it needs a noun or *the fact that*.

rows.wrong: The question is if we should continue.
rows.right: The question is whether we should continue.
rows.why: After *be* and after prepositions, use *whether*, not *if*.

rows.wrong: What I want to say that education matters.
rows.right: What I want to say is that education matters.
rows.why: A *what*-clause subject needs its own verb (*is*).

rows.wrong: I'm not sure about if it is correct.
rows.right: I'm not sure whether it is correct.
rows.why: After a preposition, use *whether*.

rows.wrong: The news which he had resigned shocked everyone.
rows.right: The news that he had resigned shocked everyone.
rows.why: The clause gives the content of *the news*, so use *that*, not *which*.

blocks.text: Pseudo-clefts with noun clauses

***What** the evidence suggests **is that** the effect fades over time.* The wh-clause sets up expectation; the that-clause delivers the point. This structure is powerful in conclusions but loses force if repeated.
Mandative that-clauses
After verbs and nouns of demand and recommendation, formal English uses the base form: *The committee recommends **that** the policy **be** reviewed.* (See the subjunctive lesson.)
Noun clauses and hedging

Embedding a claim in a that-clause lets you attribute and qualify it: *It **appears** that ..., There is **some evidence** that ..., One **possible** explanation is that ...*. This is a central technique of academic stance.

items: Noun clauses function as subject, object, complement, prepositional object or appositive.
That-clauses report facts and claims; wh- and whether-clauses report unknowns and questions.
Use statement word order inside wh- and whether-clauses.
After prepositions use wh-/whether-clauses or *the fact that*, never a bare that-clause.
*Whether* (not *if*) as subject, after prepositions, before to-infinitives and with *or not*.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Participle clauses and reduced relative clauses
summary: Participle clauses compress information: they replace a full clause with an -ing, -ed or having + past participle form. They make writing denser and more formal, and they also reduce relative clauses.

blocks.text: A participle clause packs a whole clause into a few words, without a subject or a full verb. It lets you link ideas (time, reason, result) or describe a noun concisely, which is why it is typical of good written English.

*-ing* = active (the subject does it) · past participle = passive (the subject receives it) · *having* + past participle = it happened earlier. The subject of the participle must be the subject of the main clause.

items.en: **Feeling tired**, she went to bed early.
The man **sitting by the window** is my tutor.
**Written in 1850**, the novel still feels modern.

blocks.text: A participle clause is a clause without a subject and without a full verb. It is built on a **present participle** (*-ing*), a **past participle** (*-ed / V3*) or a **perfect participle** (*having + V3*). It can describe time, reason, result, condition or add information about a noun.

items.en: **Feeling tired**, she went to bed early.
The man **sitting by the window** is my tutor.

head: Form
Meaning
Example
rows: ***Built** in 1890, the bridge is still in use.*
***Not knowing** what to do, I called my mother.*

sections.title: Adverbial participle clauses: time, reason, result, condition

items.en: **After graduating**, she moved to Toronto.
**Being** the eldest, he had to look after the others.
The storm destroyed the bridge, **cutting off** the village.
**Used** correctly, the device is completely safe.
**While waiting** for the bus, I read the news.

blocks.text: A defining or non-defining relative clause can often be reduced:

head: Full relative clause
Reduced
rows: The woman **who is speaking** is a judge.
The first person **to arrive**… (infinitive after *first, last, only*, superlatives)

blocks.text: Use *-ing* for active meaning even with past events: *The man **driving** the car was injured* (who was driving). Do not reduce with the perfect: ~~The people having attended~~ → *The people who had attended*.

items.en: The people **interviewing** the candidates…
The people **interviewed** for the study…
**Opening** the door, she saw the parcel.
**Having opened** the door, she went back to the kitchen.

rows.wrong: Walking down the street, the rain started.
rows.right: Walking down the street, I got caught in the rain.
rows.why: The participle needs the same subject as the main clause; the rain was not walking.

rows.wrong: The books writing by him are popular.
rows.right: The books written by him are popular.
rows.why: The books receive the action, so use the past participle.

rows.wrong: Having lived in Paris, she lives there for ten years.
rows.right: Having lived in Paris for ten years, she speaks fluent French.
rows.why: *Having* + past participle describes an earlier action that leads to the main clause.

rows.wrong: Being a sunny day, we went to the beach.
rows.right: It being a sunny day, we went to the beach. / As it was a sunny day, we went to the beach.
rows.why: The day was sunny, not *we*: give the participle its own subject or use a full clause.

rows.wrong: Finishing the report, she had sent it to her boss.
rows.right: Having finished the report, she sent it to her boss.
rows.why: To show that one action was completed before another, use *having* + past participle.

items: Participle clauses with their own subject (absolute constructions, formal/literary): ***The work finished**, we went home.* ***Weather permitting**, the match will go ahead.*
Fixed participle expressions: *generally speaking, judging by, considering, given (that), assuming (that), provided*.
*With* + noun + participle: ***With prices rising**, families are cutting back.*

blocks.text: Participle clauses are common in academic, journalistic and descriptive writing: *Drawing on survey data, this study examines… / Compared with 2010, unemployment has fallen.* In conversation, full clauses are more natural.

items: -ing = active; V3 = passive; having + V3 = earlier action.
They replace adverbial clauses (time, reason, condition, result) and relative clauses.
The implied subject must match the main clause subject.
*first/last/only* + to-infinitive in reduced relatives.

check.explanation: Reduced relative clause: *who is talking* → *talking*.

check.model: *Having read* shows that I finished the report before calling. *Reading* suggests the two actions happened at the same time.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: The passive, impersonal passives and the causative
summary: The passive lets you choose what a sentence is about and leave out who did the action. Advanced forms include impersonal reporting passives, passive infinitives and -ing forms, get-passives and causatives.

blocks.text: In an active sentence the subject does the action; in a passive sentence the subject **receives** it. You choose the passive to control what the sentence is about: the thing affected becomes the topic, and the doer can disappear.
Passive = *be* + past participle. The tense is shown by *be*: *is built, was built, has been built, will be built*.

items.en: Someone stole my bike. → My bike **was stolen**.
items.note: the bike is the topic; the thief is unknown

items.en: The study **was funded** by the EU.
items.note: the agent is added with *by* only when it matters

blocks.text: The causative (*have/get something done*) is related: the subject arranges the action, but someone else does it: *I had my laptop repaired.*

In an active sentence the subject does the action; in a passive sentence the subject **receives** it. Use the passive when the agent is unknown, obvious, unimportant, or when you want to keep the focus on a topic already mentioned.

items.en: The bridge **was built** in 1890.
items.note: who built it is not important here

items.en: Penicillin was discovered in 1928. It **was later developed** into a mass-produced drug.

blocks.text: *be* (in the correct tense) + past participle.

head: Tense
Passive
rows: will be made / must be made / should have been made
to be made / to have been made / being made / having been made

blocks.text: Add the agent with *by* only when it is new or important: *The novel was written **by a 19-year-old**.*
With verbs such as *say, believe, think, report, expect, know, consider, allege*, there are two patterns:

head: Pattern
Example
rows: ***It is believed that*** the painting is a fake.
*The painting **is believed to be** a fake.*
*The thieves **are thought to have escaped** by boat.*
*The minister **is said to be considering** resigning.*

items.en: Nobody likes **being criticised** in public.
The forms need **to be signed** by Friday.
She expects **to have been promoted** by then.
He **got fired** for being late.
items.note: get-passive: informal; often sudden or unwelcome events

blocks.text: *need + -ing* has passive meaning in British English: *The car needs washing* = needs to be washed.

sections.title: The causative: have and get something done

blocks.text: Use **have/get + object + past participle** when you arrange for someone else to do something, or when something unpleasant happens to you:

items.en: I'm **having my hair cut** tomorrow.
items.note: I pay someone to cut it

items.en: She **got her bag stolen** on the train.

blocks.text: Related active patterns: **have someone do** (*I had the mechanic check the brakes*), **get someone to do** (*I got my brother to help me*).

items.en: I cut my hair.
I had my hair cut.
The report was written last week.
The report got written in the end.

rows.wrong: The meeting was happened on Monday.
rows.right: The meeting happened on Monday.
rows.why: Verbs with no object (*happen, arrive, die, occur*) cannot be passive.

rows.wrong: It is said that he to be rich.
rows.right: It is said that he is rich. / He is said to be rich.
rows.why: These are two different patterns; do not mix them.

rows.wrong: I must repair my car tomorrow at the garage.
rows.right: I must have my car repaired tomorrow.
rows.why: If someone else does the work for you, use the causative.

rows.wrong: The results were analysed by us carefully.
rows.right: We analysed the results carefully. / The results were analysed carefully.
rows.why: Do not add *by* + a pronoun; either use the active or leave the agent out.

rows.wrong: This house was build in 1890.
rows.right: This house was built in 1890.
rows.why: The passive needs the past participle, not the base form.

blocks.text: Academic and scientific writing uses the passive to focus on processes and results: *Samples were collected from 40 sites and analysed.* Impersonal passives distance the writer from claims: *It has been argued that…*, *X is widely regarded as…*. Don't overuse it: a mix of active and passive reads more clearly.

items: Passive = be + past participle; agent with *by* only if useful.
*It is said that… / X is said to…*; past: *is said to have done*.
Passive infinitive and -ing forms after verbs and prepositions.
Causative *have/get something done*; *get* is more informal.

sentences.note: passive: the building is the topic; who closed it is obvious

sentences.note: present perfect passive: results that matter now

The work [[is being carried out]] by a firm that specialises in historic buildings.

check.explanation: Someone else is repairing it for me: the causative *have something done*.

check.model: The passive keeps the focus on the process and the material rather than on the researchers, which is the convention in many scientific methods sections.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Present perfect and aspect: simple, continuous and perfect forms
summary: Tense tells you when; aspect tells you how the speaker sees an action: complete, in progress, or connected to a later moment. Mastering aspect is what makes advanced English sound precise.

blocks.text: The present perfect connects a past event to **now**. You use it when what happened before still matters at the moment of speaking: a result you can see, an experience you have, or a situation that started earlier and is still true.
Present perfect = a past event seen from the present. Past simple = a past event seen in the past, cut off from now.

items.en: I**'ve lost** my keys.
items.note: The loss is in the past, but the problem is now: I can't get in.

items.en: I **lost** my keys last week.
items.note: A finished event at a finished time: we are telling a story, not describing now.

blocks.text: Ask yourself one question: *am I talking about now, or about then?* If the answer is "now" and no finished time is mentioned, the present perfect is usually right.
This lesson builds the idea in three steps, so you meet one contrast at a time:

items: **Step 1, perfect or past?** *I've finished* (relevant now) versus *I finished at six* (a finished time). See parts B and E.
**Step 2, result or activity?** *I've painted the kitchen* (the result) versus *I've been painting the kitchen* (the activity, perhaps unfinished). See part B.
**Step 3, the wider system.** The same logic (complete, in progress, connected to a later point) runs through all English tenses. See part H.

blocks.title: The aspect system in one view

blocks.text: English verbs combine **tense** (present or past) with **aspect**, which shows how the speaker views the action:

items: **Simple**: a complete whole or a fact: *I read the report.*
**Continuous** (*be* + *-ing*): in progress, temporary or unfinished: *I was reading the report when you called.*
**Perfect** (*have* + past participle): seen from a later point and connected to it: *I've read the report, so I can comment.*
**Perfect continuous**: an activity up to a point, with the focus on duration: *I've been reading reports all morning.*

blocks.text: Present perfect = **have/has + past participle**. Present perfect continuous = **have/has been + -ing**. The auxiliary *have* does all the grammatical work: it carries negation, questions and short answers.
Affirmative
Negative
Questions
Short answers
Short answers repeat only the auxiliary: ~~Yes, I have seen~~ → *Yes, I have.*

blocks.title: The whole perfect family at a glance

head: Form
Structure
Example
rows: I **had been waiting** for an hour.

blocks.title: Spelling of past participles and -ing forms

items: Regular verbs add *-ed*: *work → worked*, *study → studied*, *stop → stopped*.
Irregular participles must be learned: *go → gone*, *write → written*, *take → taken*, *be → been*.
*-ing*: drop silent *-e* (*make → making*), double a final consonant after a short stressed vowel (*run → running*, *begin → beginning*).

sections.title: Main rules: present perfect simple vs past simple

blocks.text: Use the **present perfect** when the past action is connected to now and no finished time is given:

items: experience in an unfinished period: *I've visited Kazan twice.*
a recent change with a present result: *The price has gone up.*
states up to now with *for/since*: *We've known each other since school.*

blocks.text: Use the **past simple** with a finished time or when the story is clearly in the past:

items.en: I **lived** in Berlin in 2019.
~~I have lived in Berlin in 2019.~~
items.note: A finished time expression needs the past simple.

items.en: **Have you seen** the new exhibition? ~ Yes, I **went** last week.
items.note: The conversation starts in the present perfect, then moves to past simple for details.

blocks.text: Expressions that mean "up to now" go with the present perfect. Expressions that point to a **finished** time go with the past simple.

head: Present perfect
Past simple
rows: **this week / today / this year** (period not finished)

blocks.text: Where the adverbs go

items.en: I've **just** sent it.
items.note: *just, already, ever, never* go between *have* and the participle.

items.en: Have you finished **yet**? / I haven't finished **yet**.
items.note: *yet* goes at the end in questions and negatives.

items.en: She's **already** left. / Has she left **already**?
items.note: *already* at the end of a question shows surprise.

items.en: We've lived here **for** ten years / **since** 2015.

items: *for* + length of time: *for a week*, *for ages*.
*since* + point in time: *since Monday*, *since I moved*.
*ago* = back from now, past simple only: *a week ago* (~~I've arrived a week ago~~).

blocks.text: *How long* + present perfect asks about duration up to now; *When* asks about a finished moment and needs the past simple: ~~When have you arrived?~~ → *When did you arrive?*

sections.title: Simple or continuous? Results versus activity

blocks.text: The **simple** form focuses on the result or quantity; the **continuous** form focuses on the activity, its duration, or the fact that it may be unfinished.

items.en: I**'ve painted** the kitchen.
items.note: Finished: the result is a painted kitchen.

items.en: I**'ve been painting** the kitchen.
items.note: Activity: maybe unfinished; explains paint on my clothes.

items.en: She**'s written** 2,000 words today.
~~She's been writing 2,000 words today.~~
items.note: Don't use continuous with a completed number.

blocks.text: **State verbs** (*know, believe, own, belong, seem, consist*) are normally not used in the continuous: *I've known her for years*, not ~~I've been knowing~~.

items: **Repeated actions**: *He's been calling me all week* (irritation, repetition).
**Temporary situations**: *I'm living with my parents at the moment* versus *I live in Riga* (permanent).
**Dynamic uses of state verbs** change meaning: *I'm thinking about it* (considering) / *I think so* (opinion); *She's having lunch* (eating) / *She has a car* (owns).
**This is the first time…** requires the present perfect: *This is the first time I've flown business class.*

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: *How long have you been learning English?*
asks about duration up to now
she is there now or on her way
*I've been working here for two years.*
almost the same; continuous stresses the ongoing activity

rows.wrong: I am living here since 2018.
rows.right: I've lived here since 2018. / I've been living here since 2018.
rows.why: A situation that started in the past and continues now needs the present perfect. The present tense (as in Russian *я живу здесь с 2018 года*) only describes now.

rows.wrong: When have you arrived?
rows.right: When did you arrive?
rows.why: *When* asks about a finished moment, so it needs the past simple.

rows.wrong: I have seen him yesterday.
rows.right: I saw him yesterday.
rows.why: A finished time expression (*yesterday, last week, in 2019, ago*) cuts the event off from now.

rows.wrong: I've been knowing him for years.
rows.right: I've known him for years.
rows.why: *Know* is a state verb: it describes a state, not an activity, so it is not used in the continuous.

rows.wrong: Since three years I work here.
rows.right: I've worked here for three years.
rows.why: *For* + a period, *since* + a starting point; the situation continues, so the present perfect.

rows.wrong: She's been writing 2,000 words today.
rows.right: She's written 2,000 words today.
rows.why: A completed number or quantity focuses on the result, so use the simple form.

blocks.text: At C1, aspect becomes a **choice that shapes meaning and tone**:

items: The continuous can sound **less direct and more polite**: *I was wondering if you could help* (softer than *I wondered*).
The continuous can show **annoyance**: *You're always interrupting me.*
The present perfect is used in news to **introduce** a story, then the past simple gives details: *A major earthquake has struck the region. It hit at 3 a.m.*
The perfect aspect in non-finite forms: *Having finished the report, she left*; *She seems to have forgotten.*

items.en: I**'ve been meaning** to call you.
items.note: continuous perfect for an intention that hasn't happened yet

blocks.text: Academic writing uses the present perfect to **summarise research up to now** and the past simple for **a specific study**:

items.en: Several studies **have examined** the link between sleep and memory. Walker (2017) **found** that…

blocks.text: In academic prose, the present perfect continuous is rarer; prefer *Research has increasingly focused on…* to ~~Researchers have been looking at…~~.

items: Simple = complete whole or fact; continuous = in progress or temporary; perfect = connected to a later point.
Present perfect for unfinished periods and present relevance; past simple for finished times.
Simple for results and quantities; continuous for activity and duration.
State verbs avoid the continuous unless the meaning changes.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Perfect and passive infinitives and -ing forms: to have done, being done, having been done
summary: Infinitives and -ing forms can show time and voice too. Learn how "to have done", "being asked" and "having been told" add earlier time and passive meaning, and why they make advanced writing precise and compact.

blocks.text: Infinitives (*to do*) and *-ing* forms have no tense, but they can still show **time** and **voice**. A perfect form shows that something happened earlier; a passive form shows that the subject receives the action.

Two steps: **time**: same time → *to do / doing*; earlier → *to have done / having done*. **Voice**: subject does it → active; subject receives it → *to be done / being done / to have been done / having been done*.

items.en: She seems **to know** the answer.
She seems **to have left**.
He hates **being interrupted**.
**Having been warned**, they took precautions.

blocks.text: Finite verbs show time and voice through tense and *be* + past participle: *He **was told**. She **has finished**.* But many structures need a **non-finite** form — an infinitive (*to do*) or an *-ing* form (*doing*) — after verbs, adjectives, prepositions and in reporting patterns. These forms can also carry **perfect** meaning (an earlier time) and **passive** meaning (the subject receives the action):

items: *I'd like **to be consulted**.* (passive infinitive)
*She seems **to have left**.* (perfect infinitive)
*He hates **being interrupted**.* (passive -ing)
***Having been warned**, they took precautions.* (perfect passive -ing)

blocks.text: Choose the non-finite form in two steps: **time** (same time → simple; earlier time → perfect) and **voice** (subject does it → active; subject receives it → passive).

sections.title: How it works: time and voice without tense

blocks.text: A non-finite verb has no tense of its own, so its time is understood **relative to the main verb**.

items: A **simple** form shows the same time or a later time: *She seems **to know** the answer* (now). *I hope **to finish** soon* (later).

A **perfect** form (*to have done, having done*) shows an **earlier** time, or completion before a point: *She seems **to have known** the answer all along* (earlier). *I hope **to have finished** by June* (completed before June).
A **passive** form (*to be done, being done*) shows that the subject is affected by the action: *Nobody likes **being criticised** in public.*
The **continuous** infinitive (*to be doing*) shows an action in progress: *He seems **to be working** late again.*

blocks.text: The forms combine, giving eight possibilities, though the perfect passive continuous is very rare.
Negatives place *not* before the non-finite form: *I regret **not having asked**. She pretended **not to have heard**.*
1. After seem, appear, happen, tend, claim, pretend

These verbs are followed by an infinitive whose time is relative to the main verb. Compare *He **seems to be** happy* (now) with *He **seems to have been** happy there* (earlier) and *He **seemed to have forgotten** us* (earlier than a past moment).
2. Passive reporting structures
With *say, believe, think, know, report, expect, consider, estimate*, the pattern **subject + passive reporting verb + to-infinitive** is common in news and academic writing:

items: *The painting **is believed to be** a forgery.* (belief now, about now)
*The fire **is thought to have started** in the kitchen.* (belief now, about the past)
*The company **is reported to be negotiating** a merger.* (in progress)
*Two people **are known to have been injured**.* (past + passive)

blocks.text: 3. After verbs and prepositions that take -ing

After *avoid, deny, admit, remember, regret, resent, risk, mind*, and after any preposition, use *being done* for passive meaning and *having done* to stress an earlier action: *She **denied having taken** the documents. They **complained about being kept** waiting. He **resented not being invited**.* With *deny, admit, regret, remember*, the simple -ing often already implies an earlier time, so *having* is a choice for emphasis: *He admitted **taking** / **having taken** the money.*
4. After adjectives and nouns
*It's a privilege **to have been chosen**. I was lucky **to be offered** the job. There's a risk of **being misunderstood**.*
5. Perfect infinitive after modal-like and unreal expressions

Perfect infinitives express unreal or unfulfilled past events after *would like, would rather, would hate, was/were to, was supposed to, meant to*: *I **would like to have seen** her face* (but I didn't). *They **were to have married** in June* (but the wedding was cancelled).
6. Perfect participle clauses

*Having + past participle* at the start of a sentence shows that one action was completed before another, and is typical of formal narrative and reports: ***Having reviewed** the evidence, the panel recommended no further action.* ***Having been rejected** twice, he finally won the grant.*

items.en: The bridge **is expected to be completed** next spring.
The ship **is thought to have sunk** in a storm in 1847.
items.note: present belief about a past event: perfect infinitive

items.en: She doesn't like **being told** what to do.
I'm sorry **to have kept** you waiting.
**Having lived** abroad for years, she found the return difficult.
The documents appear **to have been altered** after signing.
items.note: perfect passive: earlier, and the documents were affected

items.en: He claims **to be writing** a novel.
items.note: in progress at the time of claiming

items.en: I would rather **not have known**.
items.note: unreal past: I did know, and I wish I hadn't

head: Pair
Difference
rows: *He seems to work hard* vs *He seems to be working hard*
*She is said to live in Rome* vs *She is said to have lived in Rome*
*It is said that…* vs *X is said to…*
same meaning; the personal construction (*X is said to*) puts the topic first and is more compact.
*I remember telling him* vs *I remember being told*
I told him vs someone told me.
both show sequence; *having finished* is more formal and works without a preposition.
*I'd like to see it* vs *I'd like to have seen it*
a present/future wish vs regret about the past.

blocks.text: Passive reporting structures (*is believed to, is estimated to have*) and perfect participle clauses are hallmarks of formal writing: they make claims impersonal and compress two clauses into one. In conversation, people usually say *They think the fire started in the kitchen* or *After I'd read it, I…*.
Avoid stacking several non-finite forms in one sentence (*Having been asked to have been seen…*): this sounds heavy even in academic prose. Use a finite clause instead.

rows.wrong: He is said to be born in Vienna.
rows.right: He is said to have been born in Vienna.
rows.why: The birth happened in the past (earlier) and he received the action (passive): *to have been born*.

rows.wrong: Having finished the report, the computer crashed.
rows.right: When I had finished the report, the computer crashed.
rows.why: A perfect participle clause must share the subject of the main clause; the computer did not finish the report.

rows.wrong: She denied to have taken the money.
rows.right: She denied taking the money. / She denied having taken the money.
rows.why: *Deny* is followed by an *-ing* form, never by an infinitive.

rows.wrong: The suspect is believed having left the country.
rows.right: The suspect is believed to have left the country.
rows.why: *Be believed / said / thought* is followed by a *to*-infinitive.

rows.wrong: I don't like to be shouted.
rows.right: I don't like being shouted at. / I don't like to be shouted at.
rows.why: Keep the preposition in a passive form: *shout at someone* → *be shouted at*.

blocks.text: A perfect participle clause must share the subject of the main clause. ***Having been repaired**, the engineers tested the engine* says that the engineers were repaired. Write: *Once the engine had been repaired, the engineers tested it.*
Hedged reporting in academic writing

Passive reporting with *appear, seem* and perfect infinitives lets writers report evidence cautiously: *The effect **appears to have been overestimated** in earlier studies.* Compare the stronger *Earlier studies overestimated the effect.*
Narrative compression

Literary and journalistic prose uses perfect and passive -ing clauses to move quickly: ***Having been** turned away by three publishers, the manuscript finally appeared in 1952, **to be praised** by critics and **ignored** by readers.* The final infinitive of result (*to be praised*) is a C2 stylistic device: it presents a later, often ironic, outcome.
Was to have + past participle

*was/were to have done* describes a planned event that did **not** happen: *The minister **was to have opened** the hospital, but she fell ill.* Compare *was to open* (planned; outcome unknown or it did happen).

items: Non-finite forms show time relative to the main verb: simple = same or later time, perfect = earlier time.
Passive non-finite forms: *to be done, being done, to have been done, having been done*.
Passive reporting: *X is said / believed / thought to do / to be doing / to have done*.
*Having done* clauses show a completed earlier action and must share the main clause subject.
*Would like / was supposed to / was to* + perfect infinitive = an unfulfilled past plan or wish.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Prepositional phrases: fixed expressions beginning with a preposition
summary: Phrases such as in charge of, by mistake, on behalf of and under pressure work as single units. Knowing them makes your English more precise and idiomatic, especially in formal writing.

blocks.text: A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and works as **one fixed block** of meaning: *at risk*, *in favour of*, *on purpose*, *by mistake*. You cannot usually change the preposition or add an article, so these phrases are learned whole, like single words.
Treat each phrase as a unit: *on time* (punctual) is not *in time* (early enough); *in the end* (finally) is not *at the end of* (the final part of).

items.en: The species is **at risk of** extinction.
I deleted the file **by mistake**.
She spoke **on behalf of** the whole team.
items.note: a formal phrase used in writing and meetings

blocks.text: A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and works as one block of meaning: *at risk*, *in favour of*, *on purpose*. Many are fixed: you can't change the preposition or add an article.

items.en: The species is **at risk of** extinction.
I deleted the file **by mistake**.

Examples
rows: **at** first, **by** chance, **in** time, **on** time, **out of** order
**on the** whole, **in the** end, **at the** moment, **by the** way

Difference

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Purpose and result: in order to, so that, lest, so ... that, such ... that
summary: Purpose answers "why, with what aim?"; result answers "with what consequence?". English has a range of structures for each, from the everyday "to" to the formal "lest" and "in order that".

blocks.text: A **purpose** clause states an aim: why someone does something. A **result** clause states a consequence: what happened because of something. They can look similar (both often use *so*), so the key question is: *is this an intention or an outcome?*
Purpose: *to / in order to / so as to* + infinitive; *so that* + subject + *can/could/will/would*. Result: *so* + adjective/adverb + *that*; *such (a)* + noun + *that*.

items.en: She moved to Vienna **to be** closer to her family.
The lecture was **so** dense **that** most of us gave up.
I left early **so that** I **wouldn't** miss the train.
items.note: purpose with a different subject or a modal

blocks.text: A **purpose** clause states an intention: *She moved to Vienna **to be** closer to her family.* A **result** clause states a consequence: *The lecture was **so** dense **that** most of us gave up.* Advanced learners need a range of both, because repeating *so* and *to* makes writing monotonous, and because some structures carry formal or negative meanings that others do not.

sections.title: How it works: aim versus consequence

blocks.text: Purpose looks **forward from the agent's mind**: the outcome may or may not happen. Result looks **backward from what actually happened** (or would happen). Compare:

items.en: He left early **so that** he **would** catch the train.
He left early, **so** he caught the train.

blocks.text: The modal verb is the clue: purpose clauses with *so that / in order that* usually contain **can, could, will, would, might**, because they describe a possible future seen from the agent's point of view. Result clauses usually do not.
Negative purpose is awkward with *to*: *~~He whispered not to wake the baby~~* is possible but less clear than *so as not to wake* / *so that he wouldn't wake* / *in order not to wake*.
Purpose

head: Structure
Example
Notes
rows: in order to / so as to
more explicit; negative: *in order not to, so as not to*
*Records are kept **in order that** errors **may** be traced.*
*for* + -ing describes function, not a person's purpose
*She took notes **for fear that** she might forget.*

blocks.text: Result

head: Structure
Example
rows: *It was **such a** loud concert **that** we left.*
*There were **so many** errors **that** the paper was rejected.*
*The text is **too** long **to** read in an hour.*
so / therefore / consequently / as a result
with the result that / so much so that
*Demand rose sharply, **so much so that** prices doubled.*

blocks.text: Choosing a purpose structure

items: Same subject, positive purpose → *to* (neutral) or *in order to* (emphatic, formal).
Negative purpose → *so as not to / in order not to / so that ... not*.
Different subjects → *so that* + modal: *I'll print it **so that** you **can** read it on the train.*
Avoiding a risk → *in case* (precaution), *for fear that* (anxiety), *lest* (formal/literary).

blocks.text: Choosing a result structure

items: Degree leading to a consequence → *so ... that / such ... that*.
Excess or sufficiency → *too ... to / enough to*.
Linking sentences → *therefore, consequently, as a result, hence, thus*.

blocks.text: *Hence* and *thus* can introduce a noun phrase: *The data were incomplete, **hence** the delay.*

items.en: The scheme was simplified **so as not to** discourage small businesses.
Interviews were anonymised **so that** participants **could** speak freely.
The evidence was **so** compelling **that** the jury reached a verdict within an hour.
It was **such** an unexpected result **that** the team repeated the experiment.
Take an umbrella **in case** it rains.
The city grew rapidly, **so much so that** housing could not keep up.
The policy was unpopular and **thus** short-lived.

head: Pair
Difference
rows: *so that* (purpose, + modal) vs *, so* (result): *I saved money **so that** I could travel* / *I saved money, **so** I travelled.*
*in case* = as a precaution, before: *Bring a coat in case it's cold.* *If* = only under that condition: *Wear a coat if it's cold.*
function of a thing vs purpose of a person: *a knife **for** cutting bread* / *I used it **to** cut bread* (~~for cutting~~ is unnatural here).
*so* + adjective/adverb; *such* + (a) noun phrase: *so expensive* / *such an expensive hotel*
too = more than acceptable; enough = sufficient: *too young to vote* / *old enough to vote*

blocks.text: Neutral: *to, so that, so ... that*. Formal: *in order to, in order that, so as to, consequently, thus, hence*. Very formal or literary: *lest, for fear that, such that* (*The design is **such that** maintenance is minimal*).

In academic writing, *in order to* is often wordy: *In order to test the hypothesis, we ...* can usually be *To test the hypothesis, we ...*. Use *in order to* when the purpose needs emphasis or would otherwise be ambiguous.

rows.wrong: I came here for study English.
rows.right: I came here to study English.
rows.why: To express a purpose with a verb, use *to* + infinitive, not *for*.

rows.wrong: She saved money for to buy a car.
rows.right: She saved money to buy a car.
rows.why: *For to* is never correct; the *to*-infinitive alone already expresses the purpose.

rows.wrong: It was so a difficult exam that many failed.
rows.right: It was such a difficult exam that many failed. / The exam was so difficult that many failed.
rows.why: *So* + adjective alone; *such (a)* + adjective + noun.

rows.wrong: Take my number so that you call me.
rows.right: Take my number so that you can call me.
rows.why: *So that* normally takes a modal (*can, could, will, would*).

rows.wrong: He is enough tall to reach it.
rows.right: He is tall enough to reach it.
rows.why: *Enough* comes after an adjective but before a noun.

rows.wrong: The room was too much small.
rows.right: The room was much too small. / The room was far too small.
rows.why: Modify *too* with *much* or *far* in front of it.

blocks.text: Inverted result clauses
For emphasis: ***So** severe **was** the damage **that** the bridge had to be closed.* ***Such was** the demand **that** tickets sold out in minutes.* These inversions are formal and rhetorical.
Purpose with passive and perfect infinitives
*The rules were changed **to be seen to** act fairly.* *Measures must be taken **so as to have completed** the audit by June.* Use sparingly; clarity first.
Result without a conjunction: participle clauses

*Prices rose sharply, **causing** widespread protests.* The -ing clause presents a consequence of the whole previous clause. Make sure the implied subject is the whole situation, not a noun that cannot logically cause the result.

items: Purpose: *to, in order to, so as to, so that + modal, in order that, for fear that, lest*.
Result: *so ... that, such ... that, too ... to, enough to, so much so that, consequently, thus, hence*.
Negative purpose: *so as not to, in order not to, so that ... not*.
*In case* = precaution; *so that* + modal = aim; *, so* = result.
Formal writing: *in order that, thus, hence*; literary: *lest*.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Reported speech and reporting verbs
summary: Reporting what others say involves tense and pronoun changes, but at C1 the real skill is choosing a reporting verb that shows what the speaker did (warned, admitted, claimed) and what you think of it.

blocks.text: Reported speech gives the **content** of what someone said, inside your own sentence. Because the words now belong to a new moment and a new speaker, the details shift: pronouns, time words and often the tense move to fit the reporter's point of view.
The tense moves back when the reporting verb is past and the situation may no longer be true: *"I'm tired"* → *She said she **was** tired*. If it is still true now, you may keep the original tense.

items.en: "I'll call you tomorrow." → He said he **would** call me **the next day**.
items.note: tense, pronoun and time word all change

items.en: "The Earth goes round the Sun." → She explained that the Earth **goes** round the Sun.

blocks.text: At C1 the reporting verb matters as much as the content: *claim, admit, insist, deny* show your view of what was said.
Direct speech quotes exact words; reported (indirect) speech gives the content in your own sentence. Reporting changes **tenses, pronouns, time and place words**, and **word order** in questions.

items.en: “I'm moving to Oslo,” she said. → She said (that) she **was** moving to Oslo.

head: Direct
Reported
rows: then, that day, the next day

blocks.text: Backshift is optional when the situation is still true: *She said she **lives** in Oslo* (she still does).

items: Yes/no questions: *if / whether* + statement word order: *He asked **if I was** ready.*
Wh- questions: wh-word + statement order: *She asked **where I lived***, not ~~where did I live~~.
Orders and requests: *tell / ask* + object + (not) to-infinitive: *She told us **not to touch** anything.*

head: Pattern
Verbs
rows: agree, offer, promise, refuse, threaten, claim
advise, encourage, invite, persuade, remind, urge, warn
apologise for, insist on, object to; accuse sb of, blame sb for, congratulate sb on
acknowledge, argue, claim, explain, point out, maintain

items.en: “It was me who broke it.” → He **admitted breaking** it.
“You should see a doctor.” → She **advised me to see** a doctor.
“You lied!” → He **accused her of lying**.

blocks.text: Reporting verbs carry the writer's attitude:

items.en: The study **claims** that sugar causes hyperactivity.
The study **demonstrates** that sleep aids memory.

blocks.text: Summarising verbs: *outline, summarise, conclude, sum up, highlight, emphasise, dismiss, question*.

items.en: He **said** (that) he was tired.
He **told me** (that) he was tired.
She **suggested going** by train. / She **suggested that we go** by train.

rows.wrong: She asked me where did I work.
rows.right: She asked me where I worked.
rows.why: Reported questions use statement word order and no *do/did*.

rows.wrong: He said me that he was busy.
rows.right: He told me that he was busy. / He said (to me) that he was busy.
rows.why: *Tell* takes a personal object; *say* does not (or needs *to*).

rows.wrong: They accused him for stealing.
rows.right: They accused him of stealing.
rows.why: Each reporting verb has its own pattern: *accuse someone of* + *-ing*.

rows.wrong: She suggested me to apply.
rows.right: She suggested (that) I (should) apply. / She suggested applying.
rows.why: *Suggest* is not followed by object + *to*-infinitive.

rows.wrong: He asked if I can help him.
rows.right: He asked if I could help him.
rows.why: After a past reporting verb, *can* normally moves back to *could*.

blocks.text: Academic writing reports sources with present-tense reporting verbs: *Smith (2019) **argues** that… / As Lee **points out**,…* Choose verbs carefully: *claim* and *assert* can distance you from a source; *show* commits you to it.

items: Backshift tenses, change pronouns and time words; optional if still true.
Reported questions use statement word order.
Learn the pattern of each reporting verb.
Reporting verbs signal stance: *demonstrate* vs *claim*.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Stance adverbials and discourse markers: admittedly, arguably, to be fair, mind you
summary: Small words such as "admittedly", "arguably", "to be fair" and "that said" show your attitude, your certainty and how your ideas fit together. Learn their meaning, position and register so that you sound precise in writing and natural in conversation.

blocks.text: Stance adverbials tell the reader **how to take** a sentence. *Admittedly* concedes a weakness; *arguably* makes a claim open to debate; *frankly* signals honesty; *surprisingly* signals the unexpected. Discourse markers such as *that said* or *mind you* organise an argument or a conversation.

Choose the adverbial for its meaning, not for decoration. Concession → *admittedly, granted*. Cautious claim → *arguably, presumably*. Opinion → *frankly, personally*. Contrast with what came before → *that said, mind you*.

items.en: **Admittedly**, the sample was small.
**Arguably**, it is the best novel of the decade.
items.note: I claim this, but it can be debated

items.en: The hotel was expensive. **That said**, the service was excellent.

blocks.text: Grammar is not only about what happened; it is also about **how the speaker or writer positions themselves**. Stance adverbials comment on the whole sentence: *Admittedly, the sample was small* (I concede this), *Arguably, it is the best novel of the decade* (I claim this, but it can be debated), *Frankly, I was disappointed* (I'm being direct). Discourse markers organise interaction and argument: *That said, … / Mind you, … / As it happens, …*

A stance adverbial tells the reader **how to take** the sentence: as a concession, a cautious claim, an honest opinion, a surprise or a fact. Choosing the wrong one changes your meaning, not just your style.

sections.title: How it works: three kinds of stance

blocks.text: Grammarians group stance adverbials into three broad types.

items: **Epistemic stance** — how certain or how reliable: *undoubtedly, certainly, presumably, apparently, arguably, conceivably, in all likelihood, to some extent, in theory*.
**Attitude stance** — your evaluation or feeling: *fortunately, surprisingly, ironically, understandably, regrettably, predictably, tellingly*.
**Style stance** — how you are speaking: *frankly, honestly, to be fair, broadly speaking, in short, strictly speaking, to put it mildly*.

blocks.text: Discourse markers such as *that said, mind you, still, anyway, as it happens, by the way, in fact, actually* manage the relationship between ideas or between speakers: they concede, correct, change topic or add an unexpected point.

head: Position
Example
Effect
rows: *The plan, **to be fair**, was never fully funded.*

blocks.text: Many stance meanings can also be expressed by a clause: *It is arguable that…, There is no doubt that…, I must admit that…, To be honest, …*. The adverbial is shorter and less personal.
1. Conceding before arguing back

*Admittedly, granted, of course, true, to be fair* concede a point; a contrast marker then returns to your argument: ***Admittedly**, online courses are cheaper. **However**, completion rates remain very low.* This "yes, but" move is central to persuasive writing.
2. Making a claim that can be challenged

*Arguably* signals a strong but debatable claim; it is confident, not weak: ***Arguably**, the printing press changed society more than the internet has.* Compare *possibly* (much weaker) and *undoubtedly* (no room for debate).
3. Reporting information you have not verified

*Apparently, reportedly, allegedly, supposedly* distance the speaker from the claim: *The minister **allegedly** accepted gifts* (it is claimed; not proven). *Supposedly* often adds scepticism: *It's **supposedly** the best restaurant in town* (but I doubt it).
4. Evaluating the content

*Surprisingly, ironically, predictably, understandably, tellingly* show your reaction: ***Ironically**, the campaign against plastic produced thousands of plastic leaflets.* *Ironically* should mark a genuine contradiction between expectation and result, not just a coincidence.
5. Managing conversation

*Mind you* adds a qualifying point (informal BrE): *It's expensive. **Mind you**, it lasts for years.* *That said* concedes after a positive or negative statement: *The hotel was noisy. **That said**, the staff were wonderful.* *As it happens* introduces a relevant coincidence: *As it happens, I know the author.* *Actually* corrects or adds new information, often politely: *Actually, the meeting is on Thursday.*

items.en: **Admittedly**, the survey relied on self-reported data; **nevertheless**, the pattern is consistent across countries.
The reform was, **arguably**, the most significant change to the tax system in fifty years.
**Predictably**, the proposal was rejected by the opposition.
**To be fair**, the council had very little money to work with.
items.note: defending someone who has been criticised

items.en: The results are, **strictly speaking**, not comparable, as the samples differ.
"It's a long commute." "True. **Mind you**, the train is usually quiet."
**Apparently**, the factory will close next year.

head: Pair
Difference
rows: *arguably* = I would argue this strongly; *possibly* = it may be true (weak).
*admittedly* concedes a point against your argument; *obviously* presents a point as shared knowledge (can sound condescending).
*apparently* = I've heard / it seems; *evidently* = the evidence clearly shows.
*Hopefully, prices will fall* is standard in speech and journalism; some style guides still avoid it in formal writing.
*actually* = in fact (not "at present"); *currently* = now. A common false friend for learners.
same meaning; *that said* is shorter and slightly more formal.
*eventually* = after a long time or process; *finally* = last in a sequence or after a delay; *at last* = after impatient waiting.

blocks.text: Academic writing favours epistemic stance (*arguably, presumably, to some extent, in principle*) and cautious attitude stance (*notably, significantly, interestingly*). It avoids highly personal style markers (*frankly, honestly, to be honest*) and conversational markers (*mind you, anyway, as it happens*).

In speech, style markers (*honestly, to be fair, to be honest, I mean*) are frequent and make speakers sound engaged and natural, but repeating one marker (*to be honest… to be honest…*) sounds like a verbal tic. In professional emails, *Unfortunately*, *As it turns out* and *Just to clarify* are polite, neutral choices.

rows.wrong: Actually, the unemployment rate is 5%. (meaning "at present")
rows.right: Currently, the unemployment rate is 5%.
rows.why: *Actually* means "in fact" (often correcting something), not "now", unlike Russian *актуально* or German *aktuell*.

rows.wrong: Eventually, the company will close the factory. (meaning "possibly")
rows.right: Possibly, the company will close the factory.
rows.why: *Eventually* means "in the end, after a long time", not "possibly".

rows.wrong: Admittedly, this is the best solution.
rows.right: Arguably, this is the best solution.
rows.why: *Admittedly* concedes a weakness; it cannot introduce a strong positive claim.

rows.wrong: Ironically, it rained on the day of the picnic.
rows.right: Unfortunately, it rained on the day of the picnic.
rows.why: Bad luck is not irony; irony needs a contradiction between what is expected and what happens.

rows.wrong: To my mind, I think the policy is wrong.
rows.right: To my mind, the policy is wrong.
rows.why: Do not use two opinion markers for the same opinion.

blocks.text: Do not use *on the other hand* without a first hand: it introduces the second side of a comparison. To contrast with a previous claim, use *however*, *by contrast* or *that said*.
Layering stance for nuance

Advanced writers combine stance markers to calibrate a claim precisely: *The policy was, **admittedly**, **at least partly** successful* (concession + limited degree). *This is, **in all likelihood**, a temporary effect* (high but not total certainty).
Stance and paragraph structure

A typical argumentative paragraph moves from concession to rebuttal: ***Admittedly**, X. **However**, Y. **Indeed**, Z.* Using stance markers deliberately at these turning points makes an argument easy to follow.
Speaking: buying time and softening
In spontaneous speech, *Well, actually, …* and *I mean, …* soften disagreement; *To be fair, …* shows balance. Used sparingly, they make a speaker sound fluent and diplomatic rather than hesitant.

items: Epistemic stance: certainty and reliability (*arguably, presumably, apparently, undoubtedly*).
Attitude stance: evaluation (*surprisingly, ironically, understandably, regrettably*).
Style stance: manner of speaking (*frankly, strictly speaking, to be fair, in short*).
Concession pattern: *Admittedly / Granted, X. However, Y.*
False friends: *actually* ≠ currently; *eventually* ≠ possibly.
Academic writing: epistemic and cautious markers; speech: style and conversational markers.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Stative and dynamic verbs: meaning, aspect and change
summary: Some verbs describe states rather than actions, and states normally resist the continuous. Advanced users know when that "rule" bends, and why the continuous then changes the meaning.

blocks.text: Some verbs describe **actions and events** that unfold over time (*write, run, explain, become*). Others describe **states**: conditions that simply exist (*know, belong, contain, seem*). Continuous forms show something in progress or temporary, so they fit actions naturally but usually clash with states.
Ask: *is this something happening, or something that just is?* Happening → continuous possible. Just is → simple form.

items.en: She**'s writing** a report.
She **knows** the answer.
items.note: a state: knowing does not unfold step by step

blocks.text: Many verbs have both uses. *Think* is a state in *I think so* (an opinion) but an action in *I'm thinking about it* (considering). The meaning decides, not the verb itself.

Verbs describe either **actions and events** (dynamic: *run, write, explain, become*) or **states** (stative: *know, belong, contain, seem*). The difference matters because continuous forms present a situation as **in progress, temporary or developing**, and a state is usually none of those things. *I know the answer* describes a stable condition; *~~I'm knowing the answer~~* makes no sense because knowing does not unfold over time.
A verb is not "stative" in the dictionary. A **use** of a verb is stative or dynamic. *Have* is stative in *I have two sisters* but dynamic in *I'm having lunch*.

sections.title: How it works: why states resist the continuous

blocks.text: The continuous (be + -ing) adds three possible meanings: **duration in progress** (*she's writing*), **temporariness** (*I'm living with friends this month*) and **change or development** (*it's getting colder*). States are, by default, unbounded and unchanging, so none of these meanings applies. That is why learners are taught to avoid the continuous with verbs of:

items: **thinking and knowing**: *know, believe, understand, realise, suppose, doubt, recognise*
**feeling and wanting**: *like, love, hate, prefer, want, wish, need*
**possession and relation**: *own, belong, possess, include, contain, consist of, depend on, involve, lack*
**perception (involuntary)**: *see, hear, smell, taste* (as states)
**being and appearance**: *be, seem, appear, resemble, mean, matter, deserve*

blocks.text: When a speaker *does* use the continuous with one of these verbs, it is a deliberate choice: the state is being reframed as an **activity**, as **temporary**, as **changing**, or as **intensely felt right now**. The grammar is not broken; the meaning has shifted.

head: Verb
Stative use (simple)
Dynamic use (continuous possible)
rows: mental activity: *I'**m thinking** about changing jobs.*
experience, action: *We'**re having** a meeting / a hard time.*
temporary behaviour: *He'**s being** rude* (today, on purpose).
perform, take part: *She'**s appearing** in a new play.*
wait for: *We'**re expecting** a baby / a delivery.*
(informal) progressive of uncertainty: *It's **depending** more and more on exports.* (change)

sections.title: Main uses: when the continuous is possible with states

blocks.text: 1. Temporary or untypical behaviour
*Be* + adjective of behaviour in the continuous describes conduct at a particular time, often deliberate: *You'**re being** very unreasonable.* Compare *You **are** unreasonable* (your character).
2. Change and development

States that are changing can take the continuous, especially with comparatives: *I'**m understanding** more of each lecture as the term goes on.* *Prices **are seeming** less important to buyers than reliability.* The continuous here describes a process.
3. Emphasis on the present moment or strong feeling

In informal speech: *I'**m loving** this course* (enjoying it right now, intensely); *I'**m wanting** to leave soon* (a tentative, softened wish). This is natural in conversation but marked in formal writing.
4. Politeness and tentativeness
The past continuous or present continuous softens a request: *I **was wondering** if you could help.* *We'**re hoping** you'll join us.* Distance in time or aspect creates social distance.
5. Perfect continuous with states of duration

A few states that describe a lasting relationship accept the perfect continuous when duration is stressed: *I'**ve been wanting** to tell you this for weeks.* *She'**s been having** doubts about the project.* Most others prefer the perfect simple: *I'**ve known** him for years* (~~have been knowing~~).

items.en: The committee **consists of** twelve members.
The data **suggest** that attendance falls in winter.
Researchers **are increasingly recognising** the role of sleep in memory.
items.note: a developing trend, so continuous with an adverb of change

items.en: I **was thinking** we could split the bill.
The new manager **is proving** surprisingly popular.
items.note: prove = turn out to be, developing over time

items.en: He**'s being** deliberately vague, which isn't like him.
items.note: temporary behaviour, contrasted with his character

items.en: I **see** what you mean, but I'**m** still **seeing** the dentist on Friday.

rows: opinion vs active consideration. *I'm thinking we should leave* is an informal, tentative opinion.
*She is difficult* vs *She is being difficult*
character vs behaviour now. The second often implies the behaviour is unusual or deliberate.
the second is not used. Duration with most states uses the perfect simple.
the second only describes a developing dependency (rare, informal).
for perception in progress, English uses **can** + see/hear: *I can hear music* (not *~~I'm hearing music~~*). *I'm hearing* means *I'm being told* (*I'm hearing good things about her*).

blocks.text: In academic writing, use stative verbs in the simple form for claims: *The findings **indicate**, the model **assumes**, the sample **comprises**.* The continuous of a stative verb sounds conversational.

Informal speech uses stative continuous for **vividness**: *I'm loving it, I'm needing a break, I'm not liking this.* These are acceptable in casual conversation and marketing but avoid them in essays. In narrative, *was being* + adjective can characterise a moment: *She was being kind, not honest.*

rows.wrong: I am knowing him since 2019.
rows.right: I have known him since 2019.
rows.why: *Know* is a state; a state that began in the past and continues takes the present perfect simple.

rows.wrong: This box is containing old letters.
rows.right: This box contains old letters.
rows.why: *Contain* describes what something consists of, a state, so the simple form is used.

rows.wrong: I am agree with the author.
rows.right: I agree with the author.
rows.why: *Agree* is a verb, not an adjective, so it needs no *be*.

rows.wrong: I'm hearing a strange noise.
rows.right: I can hear a strange noise.
rows.why: Perception verbs (*hear, see, smell*) normally use *can* to describe what you perceive at the moment.

rows.wrong: The results are depending on the sample size.
rows.right: The results depend on the sample size.
rows.why: *Depend* expresses a permanent relationship, a state.

blocks.text: Over-correcting is also a mistake: *We're having a meeting* and *I'm thinking about it* are correct, because *have* and *think* describe actions here.
Stative passives and resultative states

*The door **is locked*** can describe a state (it is locked now) rather than an action. Compare *The door **is locked** every night at ten* (a repeated action). Advanced writers exploit this: *The region **is** largely **populated** by farmers* is stative; *is being populated* would describe a process of settlement.
Dynamic uses for stance

Verbs of cognition in the continuous can signal that a view is **provisional**: *Many economists **are questioning** whether growth targets are realistic.* The continuous presents the questioning as current and evolving, which is useful for describing debates.
Aspect and politeness scale
*I want → I'd like → I was wondering if → I was hoping you might*: each step adds distance (modal, past, continuous). Choose the degree that matches the social situation.

items: Stative uses describe unchanging conditions and normally take simple forms; dynamic uses describe actions and accept the continuous.
Many verbs (*think, have, see, be, taste, appear, expect*) have both uses with different meanings.
With a stative verb, the continuous signals temporariness, change, emphasis or politeness.
For duration, most states take the perfect simple: *I've known*, *it has belonged*.
Perception in progress: *can see, can hear*.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Subject–verb agreement: number, collective nouns and quantifiers
summary: Long subjects, collective nouns, quantifiers and coordinated phrases make agreement surprisingly hard. Learn the grammatical rule, the "notional" exceptions, and what careful writers choose.

blocks.text: The verb agrees with the **head noun** of its subject, not with the noun that happens to be nearest. In short sentences this is easy; in academic writing subjects are long (*The impact of these policies on rural communities…*), so the head noun can be several words away from the verb.
Find the head noun, then make the verb agree with it. *The results of the survey **show**…* (head = *results*). *The number of cars **has** risen* (head = *number*).

items.en: The **impact** of these policies on rural communities **has** been significant.
A **number** of problems **have** been reported.

blocks.text: Some nouns follow meaning rather than form: *the police **are***, *the government **is/are*** (British English allows both), *data **are/is***.

In English the verb agrees with its **subject** in number: *The report **is** late*, *The reports **are** late*. At B1 this looks trivial. At C1 it is one of the most frequent errors in academic writing, because real subjects are long (*The impact of these policies on rural communities…*), because some nouns are grammatically singular but refer to groups (*the government, the staff*), and because quantifiers and coordinated phrases follow their own logic.
Find the **head noun** of the subject and make the verb agree with it, not with the noun closest to the verb. Then check whether the meaning (notional agreement) overrides the grammar.

sections.title: How it works: grammatical and notional agreement

blocks.text: English uses two principles, and good writers know when each applies.

items: **Grammatical agreement**: the verb follows the form of the head noun. *The list of candidates **is** long* (head = *list*).

**Notional agreement**: the verb follows the meaning. *A number of candidates **have** withdrawn* (the meaning is "several candidates", so plural), *Ten kilometres **is** a long way* (one distance, so singular).
**Proximity agreement**: in a few structures the verb agrees with the nearest noun: *Either the director or the trustees **are** responsible.*

blocks.text: In formal writing, grammatical agreement is the default. Notional agreement is accepted where the meaning is clearly singular or plural, and proximity agreement is standard only after *either…or*, *neither…nor*, *not only…but also* and in *there is/are* sentences in informal speech.

head: Subject type
Verb
Example
rows: *The quality of the results **depends** on the sample.*
each of / none of / neither of + plural
*None of the proposals **was** accepted.* / *None of them **were** ready.*
most / half / all / some of + noun
*Most of the money **was** spent. Most of the funds **were** spent.*
A and B as one idea

blocks.text: 1. Long subjects: find the head

In *The rise in the cost of materials and labour **has** delayed the project*, the head is *rise*, so the verb is singular even though *materials and labour* is closest. Reading the subject aloud without its modifiers (*The rise… has delayed*) is a reliable check.
2. Collective nouns: one unit or several individuals?

Nouns such as *government, team, committee, staff, family, audience, public, police* can take a singular or plural verb in British English, depending on whether the group acts as **one body** or as **individuals**: *The committee **has** approved the budget* (a single decision); *The committee **are** divided on the issue* (members with different views). American English strongly prefers the singular. *Police, people, cattle* are always plural: *The police **are** investigating.*
In formal academic writing, choose one form and keep pronouns consistent: *The government **has** changed **its** policy* or *The government **have** changed **their** policy* — not *has… their*.
3. Quantifiers: look past "of"

With *most, all, some, half, a lot, the majority, a third, plenty* + *of*, the verb agrees with the noun that follows: *A third of the land **is** protected; a third of the species **are** endangered.* With *the majority of* + plural, plural is usual (*The majority of voters **were** undecided*), but *The majority **is** clear* (the majority as a single group) is also possible.
4. Coordination and correlatives

Two subjects joined by *and* are plural, unless they form a single idea (*Research and development **is** a priority* can be read as one function). After *or/nor*, the nearest subject wins; if that produces an awkward sentence, place the plural noun second: *Neither the chair nor the members **were** consulted.*
5. Plural-looking and Latin/Greek nouns

*News, physics, economics (the subject), measles, the United States* are singular. *Data* is plural in traditional academic style (*The data **suggest**…*) but widely singular as a mass noun (*The data **is** stored online*). *Criteria, phenomena, hypotheses* are plural; *criterion, phenomenon, hypothesis* are singular. *Statistics* is singular as a subject of study and plural for figures.

items.en: The **impact** of social media on adolescents' sleep **has** been widely studied.
**The number** of international students **has** fallen for the third year running.
**A number of** universities **have** responded by cutting fees.
**None of** the proposed solutions **addresses** the underlying problem.
The **staff are** unhappy about the new rota.
items.note: BrE plural: the staff as individuals with feelings

items.en: **What** the region needs **is** investment, not slogans.
items.note: a *what*-clause subject is singular, even before a plural complement

items.en: **Neither** the survey **nor** the interviews **were** designed to measure this.
The **data suggest** that the effect is small.

head: Pair
Difference
rows: *the number* = the figure (singular); *a number of* = several (plural).
*Each student **has**…* (singular) vs *The students each **have**…* (plural subject, *each* is an adverb).
*none of them is* vs *none of them are*
both used; *is* is more formal and expected in academic writing, *are* is normal in speech.
the family as a unit vs its members as individuals (BrE).
*There is a pen and two books* vs *There are a pen and two books*
informal English agrees with the first noun (*is*); careful writing often rewrites: *There are two books and a pen.*
*More than one student **has** complained* (singular) but *More than two students **have** complained*.

blocks.text: Academic style favours **grammatical** agreement and singular verbs after *none, neither, each* and *either*. Conversation freely uses plural (*Neither of them are coming*), and this is not a mistake in speech.

Informal speech also uses *there's* with plural nouns (*There's three reasons*), which careful writing avoids. In BrE journalism plural verbs with organisations are common (*Arsenal **are** through to the final*, *the BBC **have** apologised*); in academic and American English the singular is safer.

rows.wrong: The results of the survey shows a clear pattern.
rows.right: The results of the survey show a clear pattern.
rows.why: The head noun is *results* (plural), not *survey*.

rows.wrong: The number of cars have increased.
rows.right: The number of cars has increased.
rows.why: *The number of* has *number* as its head: singular.

rows.wrong: Every student and teacher have a card.
rows.right: Every student and teacher has a card.
rows.why: *Every* makes the subject singular.

rows.wrong: One of the main reasons are cost.
rows.right: One of the main reasons is cost.
rows.why: The head is *one*: singular.

rows.wrong: The police has arrested a suspect.
rows.right: The police have arrested a suspect.
rows.why: *Police* is always plural.

rows.wrong: These criteria is not met.
rows.right: These criteria are not met.
rows.why: *Criteria* is the plural of *criterion*.

blocks.text: Agreement in pseudo-clefts and inverted sentences

In *What worries economists **is** the falling birth rate*, the verb agrees with the *what*-clause (singular). With a plural complement, both *is* and *are* occur: *What we need **is/are** more teachers*; formal writing prefers *is*. In inversion, agreement is with the postponed subject: *Of greater concern **are** the long-term effects. Among the survivors **was** a young doctor.*
Agreement across parentheses

Parenthetical phrases do not change the subject: *The government, **like** most of its European partners, **has** resisted the proposal.* If both items should count, use *and*: *The government and most of its partners **have** resisted…*
Choosing to rewrite
When both options sound awkward (*Neither he nor I am/are…*), advanced writers rewrite: *He is not responsible, and neither am I.*

items: Agree with the **head noun**, not the nearest noun.
*The number of* + singular verb; *a number of* + plural verb.
Quantifier + *of*: agree with the noun after *of* (*most of the money is / most of the funds are*).
Collective nouns: singular for a unit, plural (BrE) for individuals; be consistent with pronouns.
*Either/neither…or/nor*: agree with the nearest subject.
Clauses, gerunds and amounts are singular.
